title: Suppressing "estimate only" message
description:
_I posted this in the lubridate's Google Groups a month ago.  I'm reposting it here, since it looks like it's the only thread in the group._

Is it currently possible to suppress the message "estimate only: convert difftimes to intervals for accuracy" when executing something like the following line?
`as.period(ymd("2010-01-01") - ymd("2009-11-01"))` #From https://github.com/hadley/lubridate/issues/75

Is there a way to suppress this specific message, without suppressing more important warnings that may occur?

If not, would t be helpful if I forked lubridate and modified this method from

```
setMethod("as.period", signature(x = "difftime"), function(x, unit = NULL, ...){
  message("estimate only: convert difftimes to intervals for accuracy")
  seconds_to_period(as.double(x, "secs"))
})
```

to something like

```
setMethod("as.period", signature(x = "difftime"), function(x, unit = NULL, showAccuracyWarning=TRUE, ...){
  if( showAccuracyWarning ) message("estimate only: convert difftimes to intervals for accuracy")
  seconds_to_period(as.double(x, "secs"))
})
```

?

To make the signatures and behavior consistent, I suppose these two lines show be modified as well.
https://github.com/hadley/lubridate/blob/95418730b7beff3508f7044a4ce11326167afc81/R/coercion.r#L370
https://github.com/hadley/lubridate/blob/95418730b7beff3508f7044a4ce11326167afc81/R/coercion.r#L436

I really like the period concept in lubridate.  I deal with human age a lot, such as if kids were eligible for a specific government program during a past event.  The period `10y 0m 1d` is more accurate/appropriate than dividing a difftime of 3653 days by 365.25.  It's even more important when the eligibility threshold is 6 months or 34 months old.

title: Could `with_tz` take a vector of `tzones`?
description:
I have a dataframe with a column of timestamps in UTC and another column with the local timezone. I need to create new columns such as:  the timestamp converted to the local time or the number of minutes since midnight in the local timezone. 

These variables are useful when looking at travel behavior. Working in relation to the local time zone rather than strictly using UTC is essential to the analysis.

Here is an example dataframe.

``` r
library(dplyr)
data <- data_frame(
  timestamp_utc = as.POSIXct(c('2015-11-18 03:55:04', '2015-11-18 03:55:08', 
                    '2015-11-18 03:55:10'), tz = "UTC"),
  local_tz = c('America/New_York', 'America/Los_Angeles', 
               'America/Indiana/Indianapolis')
  )
```

I'd like to be able to use something like `with_tz`, but it doesn't work in a chain of other `dplyr` statements due to the fact that `tzone` cannot be a vector.

``` r
mutate(data, timestamp_local = with_tz(timestamp_utc, tzone = local_tz))
```

I've created a work around, but it is slow (see [StackOverflow](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/33848563/with-tz-with-a-vector-of-timezones/33848764#33848764)). With this method, the result has to be a string, otherwise `unlist()` or `c()` will turn the result back to the system timezone, which in this case is UTC.

``` r
get_local_time <- function(timestamp_utc, local_tz) {
  l <- lapply(seq(length(timestamp_utc)), function(x) {
    format(with_tz(timestamp_utc[x], local_tz[x]), "%FT%T%z")
  })
  unlist(l)
}

> mutate(data %>% timestamp_local = get_local_time(timestamp_utc, tzone = local_tz))
Source: local data frame [3 x 3]

        timestamp_utc                     local_tz          timestamp_local
               (time)                        (chr)                    (chr)
1 2015-11-18 03:55:04             America/New_York 2015-11-17T22:55:04-0500
2 2015-11-18 03:55:08          America/Los_Angeles 2015-11-17T19:55:08-0800
3 2015-11-18 03:55:10 America/Indiana/Indianapolis 2015-11-17T22:55:10-0500
```

Could `with_tz` take a vector of `tzones`?

title: Feature request: `int_overlaps` returning a numeric (amount), not a logical (boolean)
description:
Based on a [StackOverflow question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58517015/lubridate-find-overlap-time-between-interval-and-a-date), it seems like there should be a function that returns the **amount** of overlap, not just a logical for overlap. Like so:

```r
int_overlaps_numeric <- function (int1, int2) {
  stopifnot(c(is.interval(int1), is.interval(int2)))

  x <- intersect(int1, int2)@.Data
  x[is.na(x)] <- 0
  as.duration(x)
}

# Examples:
int1 <- as.interval(5, Sys.time())
int2 <- as.interval(5, Sys.time()+3)
int3 <- as.interval(5, Sys.time()+1000)

int_overlaps(int1, int2)
> [1] TRUE

int_overlaps_numeric(int1, int2)
> [1] "1.99399495124817s"

int_overlaps(int1, int3)
> [1] FALSE

int_overlaps_numeric(int1, int3)
> [1] "0s"
```

This can still be used in the same code as the current `int_overlaps`, since `as.logical(as.duration(30))` evaluates to `TRUE` and `as.logical(as.duration(0))` evaluates to `FALSE`.

I believe the calls to `update()` [here](https://github.com/tidyverse/lubridate/blob/45395b4b7e785ee6ec00e9e89bddc400df1b96dd/R/round.r#L281-L286) should have `days` instead of `day`, `hours` instead of `hour`, and so on.

title: Parsing oddity with ymd_hms
description:
`ymd_hms("2007-03-08 13:13",truncated=1)` gives `"2007-03-08 13:13:00 UTC"`, as expected.
`ymd_hms("2007-03-08 1:13")` gives `NA` and warning, as expected.
But `ymd_hms("2007-03-08 13:13")` gives `"2020-07-03 08:13:13 UTC"` without warning. It is using a "YYMM-DD-HH MM:SS" date format.
Maybe this is expected behaviour, but allowing that liberal a date format (specifically "-" as a separator both within the date and between the DD and HH) seems likely to lead to parsing results that the user did not expect.

(with lubridate_1.6.0 and lubridate_1.6.0.9009)

title: Consider passing through date-time objects in parser functions
description: Beginner R users often pass date-time objects to parsing functions like `ymd_hms`. This is very inefficient and can cause unexpected behavior (for example `ymd_hm` would not parse a full date). Directly returning an appropriate date-time when passed in a date-time object would avoid such issues.

title: tz function not behaving as expected
description:
A little issue: in lubridate_1.7.4 the default timezone cannot be changed by the tz function (as per the example in the documentation).  Additionally, contrary to the documentation tz() function default returns "UTC" not "GMT". When a time zone or a format with hours & mutes is  stipulated the function behaves as expected:

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate) 

## These work:
# ymd_hm("2012-03-26 01:55") 
# ymd("2012-03-26", tz = "Pacific/Fiji")

# But not the documentation example:
x <- ymd("2012-03-26")   

# returns "UTC" not "GMT" as suggested in documentation (not a big deal)
tz(x)       

# try to force change:
tz(x) <- "America/Chicago"

# returns "UTC" not "America/Chicago" as expected
tz(x) 

```

title: Documentation suggestion: specify whether %within% is inclusive

title: day("01-01-2016") returns day 20 with no warning of 4 digit input.
description:
The day() function (and week() function similarly) returns the first two digits from year in the following examples so long as those first two digits are between 1 and 31. This somewhat makes sense given it's expecting the format ymd. However, an error or warning should be present where the expected day figure is more than two digits, rather than just ignoring all extra digits.

> day("01-01-20")
[1] 20

[1] 20
> day("01-01-3016")
[1] 30
> day("01-01-3116")
[1] 31
> day("01-01-3199")
[1] 31
> day("01-01-319999999999999999")

> day("01-01-4000")
Error in as.POSIXlt.character(x, tz = tz(x)) : 
  character string is not in a standard unambiguous format

title: suggestion to add attribute "approx" to Duration class
description:
In my code, I usually define a function `to_approx_duration`:
``` r
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)

to_approx_duration <- function (time) str_replace(as.duration(time), ".*\\((.*)\\)$", "\\1")

to_approx_duration(minutes(3473))
#> [1] "~2.41 days"

to_approx_duration(hours(9939))
#> [1] "~1.13 years"
```
---
Would you consider interesting to add a public attribute `approx` to the `Duration` class?
So it would be possible to obtain something like:
``` r
as.duration(minutes(3473))$approx
#> [1] "~2.41 days"
```

title: Enhancement request: special periods for accounting
description:
I work in the world of accounting. We use "special" periods e.g. a period 14 that updates the final figures for a book year, but these amendments are made in a new fiscal year. See e.g. [special periods in SAP](https://help.sap.com/doc/saphelp_sfin100/1.10/en-US/22/52d7531a4d424de10000000a174cb4/content.htm?no_cache=true)

Could you add functionality for handling these special periods, I'm thinking of:
specifying the special period e.g. P14: starts two periods after 31/12, the Posting Date = last day of the fiscal year (eg 12/31/2019) AND if there is a special Posting Period value to 13 or 14 or 15 or 16, then these postings end up in the special period, that is ordered like P12=month 12, P13, P14, P15, P16, P1=month 1, new book year, so we have  a way to keep those adjusting entries out of period 12 but still, include them in the fiscal year?

title: Periods are not automatically normalised
description:
When adding periods, values don't increment across seconds minutes hours etc. For example, adding 45 + 16 minutes returns 61 minutes, not 1 hour 1 minute


```r
library(lubridate)
p1 <- as.period(hms("23:45:00"))
p2 <- as.period(hms("00:16:00"))
p3 <- seconds(60*16)
p1 + p3
#"23H 45M 960S"
p1 + p2
#"23H 61M 0S"
```

title: Support for 360_day, 365_day, Julian, Proleptic Gregorian calendars
description:
Climate models often use different calendars from the one we are used to. Other than the standard R calendar, 360_day, 365_day and 366_day calendars are quite common. The [CF-Conventions](http://cfconventions.org/Data/cf-conventions/cf-conventions-1.7/cf-conventions.html#calendar), which form the basis for the sharing of climate data in the netCDF format, specify the following calendars as possible:

- gregorian or standard
Mixed Gregorian/Julian calendar as defined by Udunits. This is the default.
- proleptic_gregorian
A Gregorian calendar extended to dates before 1582-10-15. That is, a year is a leap year if either (i) it is divisible by 4 but not by 100 or (ii) it is divisible by 400.
- noleap or 365_day
Gregorian calendar without leap years, i.e., all years are 365 days long.
- all_leap or 366_day
Gregorian calendar with every year being a leap year, i.e., all years are 366 days long.
- 360_day
All years are 360 days divided into 30 day months.
- julian
Julian calendar.

In R, support for these calendars is limited but not non existent: the package `PCICt` includes support and basic arithmetic for these calendars. Would it be possible somehow to include `lubridate` support for `PCICt` calendars or objects?

title: String output from Month
description:
Related to #42.

## Month is not returned as string

Docs say `the months element of x as a number (1-12) or character string.`: https://github.com/tidyverse/lubridate/blob/455a759d34e292df9b6e45bd4c888851ff94fb5e/R/accessors-month.r#L10 and https://github.com/tidyverse/lubridate/blob/455a759d34e292df9b6e45bd4c888851ff94fb5e/R/accessors-month.r#L17 

This is not the case when running the code below.  The issue is that **ordered** factors may not always be wanted from the output.  Coercion could happen on user-end or an option added.


```r
library(lubridate)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'lubridate'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     date
x <- ymd("2012-03-26")
month(x)
#> [1] 3
month(x, label = TRUE)
#> [1] Mar
#> 12 Levels: Jan < Feb < Mar < Apr < May < Jun < Jul < Aug < Sep < ... < Dec
factor(month(x, label = TRUE))
#> [1] Mar
#> Levels: Mar
month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)
#> [1] March
#> 12 Levels: January < February < March < April < May < June < ... < December
as.character(month(x, label = TRUE))
#> [1] "Mar"
```

## Ordered factors in Linear model
In a linear model, the ordered factor can cause some issues (but is known behavior).  Here we generate some data:

``` r
set.seed(20190304)
n = 100
x = ymd("2012-03-26") + rpois(n, lambda = 1000)
y = rnorm(n)
```

Running the LM for different versions

``` r
# numeric
lm(y ~ month(x))
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = y ~ month(x))
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> (Intercept)     month(x)  
#>    0.023665    -0.002057

# factor of numeric
lm(y ~ factor(month(x)))
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = y ~ factor(month(x)))
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>        (Intercept)   factor(month(x))2  factor(month(x))10  
#>           -0.01926             0.16010            -0.13490  
#> factor(month(x))11  factor(month(x))12  
#>            0.10197            -0.05638

# ordered factor
lm(y ~ month(x, label = TRUE))
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = y ~ month(x, label = TRUE))
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>              (Intercept)  month(x, label = TRUE).L  
#>                -0.005099                 -0.054042  
#> month(x, label = TRUE).Q  month(x, label = TRUE).C  
#>                -0.028072                  0.018935  
#> month(x, label = TRUE)^4  
#>                -0.228768
```

Note, the L - linear, Q- quadratic, C - cubic: this is a behavior of an ordered factor.

```r
# unordered factor - same as character but reordered due to names
lm(y ~ factor(month(x, label = TRUE), ordered = FALSE))
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = y ~ factor(month(x, label = TRUE), ordered = FALSE))
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                                        (Intercept)  
#>                                           -0.01926  
#> factor(month(x, label = TRUE), ordered = FALSE)Feb  
#>                                            0.16010  
#> factor(month(x, label = TRUE), ordered = FALSE)Oct  
#>                                           -0.13490  
#> factor(month(x, label = TRUE), ordered = FALSE)Nov  
#>                                            0.10197  
#> factor(month(x, label = TRUE), ordered = FALSE)Dec  
#>                                           -0.05638
lm(y ~ as.character(month(x, label = TRUE)))
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = y ~ as.character(month(x, label = TRUE)))
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                             (Intercept)  
#>                                -0.07564  
#> as.character(month(x, label = TRUE))Feb  
#>                                 0.21648  
#> as.character(month(x, label = TRUE))Jan  
#>                                 0.05638  
#> as.character(month(x, label = TRUE))Nov  
#>                                 0.15835  
#> as.character(month(x, label = TRUE))Oct  
#>                                -0.07851

# same with `abbr = FALSE`
lm(y ~ factor(month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)))
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = y ~ factor(month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)))
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                                    (Intercept)  
#>                                      -0.005099  
#> factor(month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)).L  
#>                                      -0.054042  
#> factor(month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)).Q  
#>                                      -0.028072  
#> factor(month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)).C  
#>                                       0.018935  
#> factor(month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE))^4  
#>                                      -0.228768
lm(y ~ as.character(month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)))
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = y ~ as.character(month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)))
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                                                (Intercept)  
#>                                                   -0.07564  
#> as.character(month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE))February  
#>                                                    0.21648  
#>  as.character(month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE))January  
#>                                                    0.05638  
#> as.character(month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE))November  
#>                                                    0.15835  
#>  as.character(month(x, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE))October  
#>                                                   -0.07851
```

## Overall

Overall, this is a behavior of an ordered factor, which makes things into
linear/quadratic/higher order variables in the regression:
https://stackoverflow.com/a/25736023/2549133. This is not a
lubridate issue per se. I’m just noting the docs different to the output.
I’m not sure as to whether 1) an argument `ordered = TRUE` for default be
added, 2) the docs changed, or 3) the output to be character as I think
more people on this thread have better experiece with that

title: Leading zero in dby date with multiple orders (dOmy, Omdy) parses incorrectly

title: Add a function for calculating an accounting calendar (4-4-5 and others)
description:
I've recently been working with a lot of data that follows a 4-4-5 accounting calendar, and I realized it would be helpful to have a function that calculates those month breaks. It seemed simple enough to implement and I thought I'd propose it as an addition.

The goal here is to calculate the date breaks for a calendar that follows a certain week pattern, that deviates from the actual calendar. In accounting 4-4-5 (4 weeks, 4 weeks, 5 weeks) is a common pattern, and other retail calendars follow similar patterns. 

`x` - a date from the first month of the desired calendar
`weekStart` - set the day of the week each break is calculated from
`pattern` - pattern of weeks, i.e. 4-5-4, 4-4-5, 4-5, etc.
`month1_weeks` - if the first month has a different number of weeks than the pattern
`firstWeek` - specify an offset if the year does not start in the first week of the month

```
accountingCalendar <- function(x, weekStart = 7, pattern = c(4,4,5), month1_weeks = NULL, firstWeek = 1){
	# get the first of the month, offset by firstWeek
	start_month <- 	floor_date(x, 'month') + weeks(firstWeek-1)

	# create a vector of weeks in each month, limit length to twelve
	# but allow for a pattern of varying length
	week_breaks <- c(0, month1_weeks, rep(pattern,12))[1:12]

	# adjust date to the start of the week based on week_start
	cal_breaks <- floor_date(start_month, 'week', 
		week_start = getOption('lubridate.week.start', weekStart))+
	# then generate the date vector by addting the cumulative vector of weeks
		weeks(cumsum(week_breaks))
	return(cal_breaks)
}
```

This is the first time I've suggested something for a R library, so I'd certainly appreciate any feedback on how to improve this as well, and how relevant it is.

title: lubridate is giving error when the leading zero is missing for either day or month in ymd format.
description:
Recently I have found that **lubridate** will give NA when the leading zero is missing for either day or month in ymd format.

For example, when you run
```R
datetest <- c("201711","2017092","2017110")
lubridate::ymd(datetest)     
[1] NA NA NA
Warning message:
All formats failed to parse. No formats found. 
```
_This will return NAs._  

For as.Date(), it is evaluating from left to right and assuming double digit for month and day. Therefore, if the day is missing a leading zero, it will still return.

Below is what I have for current situation.
```R
ymd_add_o1 <- function(date) {
  # filter out the date that has one digit in mm, as if it is two digit, as.Date() will be able to parse it
  na_date <- date[is.na(as.Date(date,format="%Y%m%d"))]
  # get the first 4 digit
  na_date_yyyy <- substr(na_date,1,4)
  # get the digit for mmdd
  na_date_mmdd <- substr(na_date,5,nchar(na_date))
  # adding 0 to date object to ensure the order of output
  date[is.na(as.Date(date,format="%Y%m%d"))] <- paste0(na_date_yyyy,"0",na_date_mmdd)
  # use as.Date() to parse the date with leading zero added
  as.Date(date,format="%Y%m%d")
}


ymd_add_o1(datetest)
[1] "2017-01-01" "2017-09-02" "2017-11-01"
```
It would be great if ymd() can have an option to add the leading zero and parse the date.

title: Relative weekday calculations: Closest wday, Next  wday, Previous wday
description:
Some business and scheduling applications require relative weekday calculations: e.g. closest Monday, 3rd Tuesday of the month, last Wednesday of the month. It would be nice if there were functions that took a date and returned the date that was the closest, next or previous weekday (Sun, Mon, Tue, etc.). I've written my own functions for this, and will make them available when I next have time, but here's the pseudocode:

Closest weekday:
Accept valid date, valid target weekday as input 
(optional input flag to return only shift duration as a lubridate interval class)
Determine weekday of input date (with lubridate::wday)
Determine shift in days as -(input wday - target wday + 4) %% 7 - 3
Add calculated shift to input date (with lubdridate::days)
Return shifted date

Next weekday:
Accept valid date, valid target weekday as input
(optional input flag to return only shift duration as a lubridate interval class) 
Determine weekday of input date (with lubridate::wday)
Determine shift in days as -(input wday - target wday) %% 7
Add calculated shift to input date (with lubdridate::days)
Return shifted date

Previous weekday:
Accept valid date, valid target weekday as input
(optional input flag to return only shift duration as a lubridate interval class) 
Determine weekday of input date (with lubridate::wday)
Determine shift in days as (input wday - target wday) %% 7 *-1
Add calculated shift to input date (with lubdridate::days)
Return shifted date

Convenience functions could also be created, e.g.: closestSunday, nextMonday, prevThurs
These generic functions could then be combined trivially with existing lubridate functions to calculate more meaningful dates that have relative dates within a month such as pay days, holidays, etc. 

I'd love some feedback on whether there is interest in incorporating functions like this into the lubridate package and if so, guidance on naming and formatting that would make the code more consistent with the other functions in the package.  Also no objection at all to someone else implementing the pseudocode above or equivalent in future versions of lubridate. I'll try to submit my own code when I have time, but I'm not sure when that will be.

title: Timezone import slow - possible solutions
description:
## Note that this first post does not in fact present a viable solution.

At the moment, tz conversion is done in force_tz.

essentially

``` R
parse_date_time(tz="America/Los_Angeles","2013-12-16 00:06:04","YmdHMS")
[1] "2013-12-16 00:06:04 PST"
```

is

``` R
force_tz(tz="America/Los_Angeles",parse_date_time("2013-12-16 00:06:04","YmdHMS"))
[1] "2013-12-16 00:06:04 PST"
```

Point 1.  The output format of both of these commands includes timezone in a format (I can't find the name of) represented by "PST".  This is neither Olson nor ISO8601.  It would be _sane_ to be able to import this representation directly back into time handling functions, but I can't see how

``` R
> parse_date_time("2013-12-16 00:06:04 PST","YmdHMSz")
[1] NA
```

nope.  Let's call this one R's problem for now, not lubridate's.

``` R
?strptime
     ‘%Z’ (output only.) Time zone as a character string (empty if not
          available).
```

Let's assume we know the timezone (or have chosen it) to be "America/Los_Angeles".  Let's also make the simplifying assumption that DST doesn't exist for the next few steps.

``` R
strftime(parse_date_time("2013-12-16 00:06:04","YmdHMS"),"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z")
[1] "2013-12-15 16:06:04 -0800"
```

This _IS_ parable, and note that the time is correct, and also that force_tz is no longer invoked (use trace(force_tz)).

``` R
parse_date_time("2013-12-15 16:06:04 -0800","YmdHMSz")
[1] "2013-12-16 00:06:04 UTC"
strftime(parse_date_time("2013-12-15 16:06:04 -0800","YmdHMSz"),"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z")
[1] "2013-12-15 16:06:04 -0800"
```

This is important because force_tz is very slow compared to parsing.

``` R
system.time(A<-parse_date_time(tz="America/Los_Angeles",rep("2013-12-15 16:06:04",1000000),"YmdHMS"))
trace: force_tz(fast_strptime(x, fmt, tz = "UTC"), tzone = tz)
   user  system elapsed 
 13.801   0.129  13.934 
system.time(B<-with_tz(tz="America/Los_Angeles",parse_date_time(rep("2013-12-15 16:06:04 -0800",1000000),"YmdHMSz")))
   user  system elapsed 
  0.332   0.049   0.380 
```

Note that I curiously have to tell it it's America/Los_Angeles anyway (using cheap with_tz call)

So, what if I have a function like:

``` R
tzoffset(tz) { return "-0800" }
```

and do

``` R
parse_date_time(paste("2013-12-16 00:06:04",tzoffset("America/Los_Angeles")),"YmdHMSz")
```

This is all probably wishful thinking, but timezone conversion is about the slowest thing in the shiny app I'm writing, and I get 50Mb+ input files.

title: pretty_dates requires unrealistic knowledge about number of intervals
description:
From David A. :

The `pretty_dates` function is limited to creating dates based on a set number of breaks. The function assumes that you know exactly the number of intervals required to get nice looking dates.

Consider your example in the documentation that creates nice dates:

```
x <- seq.Date(as.Date("2009-08-02"), by = "year", length.out = 2)
# "2009-08-02" "2010-08-02"
pretty_dates(x, 12)
```

If you change it to `pretty_dates(x, 13)`, they no longer "look pretty."  What I am getting at is that the user does not necessarily know the exact number of intervals, and he or she may not be strict about requiring exactly 13 breaks.

Can there be an argument built in to the function that indicates whether the user is strict about the breaks or not? I was thinking of something like this:

```
pretty_dates(x, 13, strict=FALSE)
## "2009-08-01 GMT" "2009-09-01 GMT" "2009-10-01 GMT"  etc.

pretty_dates(x, 20, strict=FALSE)

title: floor_date(x, unit = 'weeks') ignores lubridate.week.start option
description:
Hello,

`floor_date(x, unit = 'weeks')` returns the same value (the previous Sunday, in my testing) regardless of what the `lubridate.week.start` option is set to:

```
library(lubridate)

options(lubridate.week.start = 7)
wday(ymd('2017-01-02'))                         # 2
floor_date(ymd('2017-01-02'), unit = 'weeks')   # "2017-01-01"

options(lubridate.week.start = 1)
wday(ymd('2017-01-02'))                         # 1
floor_date(ymd('2017-01-02'), unit = 'weeks')   # "2017-01-01"
```

As the above snippet shows, even though the results of `wday(x)` change according to `lubridate.week.start`, the results of `floor_date(x, unit = 'weeks')` do not. Intuitively, if the week start is set to Sunday, then `floor_date()` should always return a Sunday; if the option is set to Monday, then the function should always return a Monday, and so on.

I believe the issue is actually due to the `update()` function also ignoring this option:

```
options(lubridate.week.start = 7)
update(ymd('2017-01-02'), wday = 1)     # "2017-01-01"
wday(ymd('2017-01-01'))                 # 1

options(lubridate.week.start = 1)
update(ymd('2017-01-02'), wday = 1)     # "2017-01-01"
wday(ymd('2017-01-01'))                 # 7
```

In the latter case, `wday(update(x, wday = 1))` does not give a result of `1`, even though we explicitly set `wday = 1`.

title: More robust format handling in ymd_hms()
description:
This works as desired:
```
> tmp <- as.POSIXct("2019-09-01 01:00:00")
> attributes(tmp)
$class
[1] "POSIXct" "POSIXt" 

$tzone
[1] ""
> ymd_hms(tmp)
[1] "2019-09-01 01:00:00 UTC"
```
But this fails:
```
> tmp <- as.POSIXct("2019-09-01 00:00:00")
> ymd_hms(tmp)
[1] NA
Warning message:
All formats failed to parse. No formats found.  
```

The failure is presumably because the coercion of `POSIXct` to character string results in omitted hh:mm:ss when it's midnight (i.e. 00:00:00). 

**Background:**
Many database access packages return datetimes as either character strings (e.g. `RMySQL`) or as `POSIXct` but without the tzone attribute set (e.g. `RMariaDB`, `RPostgres`). 

It's common practice in databases to store datetimes in UTC timezone. And the pattern of transforming query results with `ymd_hms()` is a simple way to a) convert to `POSIXct` type if character string, and b) assign UTC timezone (it's the default `tz` argument). 

As `ymd_hms()` is currently implemented, this works in all cases but for a `POSIXct` type and a time of midnight. 

There are two existing *solutions* to this:

```
> ymd_hms(tmp, truncated = 3)
[1] "2019-09-01 UTC"
```
and
```
> ymd_hms(format(tmp, format = "%F %T"))
[1] "2019-09-01 UTC"
```

But both require changes to existing code.

Would prefer that `ymd_hms()` be modified to behave more consistently with input of a `POSIXct` type and a time of midnight.

title: Suggestion to add function to find next / last weekday
description:
When dealing with dates finding the next (or last) weekday (w) of a certain date (d) is a common problem. For example: Finding the next Monday after Sep 13, 2019 (Fri) which would be Sep 16, 2019 (Mon). It would be great to have such a function in lubridate.

Below is the core (without checks of parameters w, d) of a function called `next_wday()` and ist equivalent  `last_wday() `, which make use of `lubridate::wday()`.

Would this be worth a pull request? If yes, I would give it a try and flesh out the function below.

```
# a function to find the next weekday w of date d

next_wday <- function(d, w) { 

  d + (seq(w - 1, length = 7) %% 7 + 1L)[8 - lubridate::wday(d)] 

}

# a function to find the last weekday w of date d

last_wday <- function(d, w) {
  
  d - (seq(-w, length = 7) %% 7 + 1L)[lubridate::wday(d)] 
  
}

# Example
df <- data.frame(date=seq.Date(from=as.Date('2019-09-11'), to=as.Date('2019-09-21'), by= 1))
df$next_wednesday <- next_wday(df$date, 4)
df$last_monday <- last_wday(df$date, 2)

title: Feature request: new epiweek/epiyear functions would benefit from option to use "US-CDC" defn or "isoweek"
description:
<< continuing a discussion in #492 >>

The US/CDC uses an epiweek defined as starting on Sunday.  Much of the rest of the world uses epiweeks that start on Monday (as in the definitions used by `isoweek`).

It would be helpful if the epiweek and epiyear functions had an option to permit the choice of either definition, perhaps following the  `week_start` option as in `wday`?

As well, the documentation could indicate the rationale for this option, perhaps something as simple as

"The US/CDC uses an epiweek defined as starting on Sunday.  Much of the rest of the world uses epiweeks starting on Monday -- as in the definitions used by `isoweek`.

Could these be added?

Thank you!

title: Creating nested list of periods makes all periods 7 days
description:
It looks like periods cannot be added to nested lists as all periods are converted to periods of 7 days. (The hilop argument can be removed and it doesn't change the outcome)

```r
TSLvars <- list(
  tslret = list(n = lubridate::days(7), hilop = .9),
  tslret = list(n = lubridate::weeks(2), hilop = .9),
  tslret = list(n = lubridate::weeks(4), hilop = .9),
  tslret = list(n = lubridate::weeks(12), hilop = .9))
```
I can't imagine this is intended behavior?

Strange workaround to achieve the intended effect:
```
TSLvars <- purrr::pmap(list(.x = c(7,7*2, 7*4, 7*12), .y = rep(.9,4)),~ list(n = lubridate::days(.x), hilop = .y)) %>% setNames(rep("tslret", length(.)))
```
However, as soon as that is nested into a larger list all periods revert to 7d.

*Solution*
Alright, it appears that it's caused by making the list items the same name. Solved by using different names for each list item.

title: Vectorize is.Date()
description:
Is there a specific reason why `is.Date()` is not vectorized. As far as I know, all lubridate functions are vectorized. So it seems to be a bit odd, that `is.Date()` is not. Thus, I suggest vectorizing the function for more consistency.

``` r
library(lubridate)
#> 
#> Attache Paket: 'lubridate'

dates <- c("2019-06-14", "2019-07-15")

is.Date(dates)

is_Date <- Vectorize(is.Date, USE.NAMES = FALSE)
is_Date(dates)

real_dates <- as.Date(dates)

is.Date(list(real_dates, dates))
#> [1] FALSE
is_Date(list(real_dates, dates))

title: Unit test fails on the day before the change to or from savings time.
description:
During routine testing of lubridate, I had a test failure:

Running the tests in ‘tests/testthat.R’ failed.
Last 13 lines of output:
      date
  
  ── 1. Failure: difftime comparison with periods works (@test-ops-compare.R#63)  
  days(1) == (t + days(1)) - t isn't true.
  
  ── 2. Failure: difftime comparison with periods works (@test-ops-compare.R#64)  
  (t + days(1)) - t == days(1) isn't true.
  
I instrumented the test-ops-compare.R to see why, and the problem is that tonight, the timezone changes. The test then fails. Here's the instrumented code:

```r
test_that("difftime comparison with periods works", {
    t <- now()
    print(t)
    print(days(1))
    print(t + days(1))
    print(t + days(1) - t)
  expect_true(days(1) == (t + days(1)) - t)
  expect_true((t + days(1)) - t == days(1))
})
```
and here is the output:
```r
> source("test-ops-compare.R")
[1] "2019-03-09 11:21:00 EST"
[1] "1d 0H 0M 0S"
[1] "2019-03-10 11:21:00 EDT"
Time difference of 23 hours
Error: Test failed: 'difftime comparison with periods works'
* days(1) == (t + days(1)) - t isn't true.
* (t + days(1)) - t == days(1) isn't true.
```
I suggest modifying t <- now() to instead use a fixed date that's not near a time change anywhere on earth for this test.

title: Please don't mask with depreciated functions/closures
description:
"here" is depreciated in lubridate, and has been for almost two years.  However, that doesn't stop a standard `library(lubridate)` from masking the function from package [here](https://github.com/r-lib/here).

Is there a way you (as the package people) make lubridate library loads not clobber other packages functions with a depreciated lubridate function?  For the end user there's always `here <- here::here` after the library loads, but IMHO lubridate shouldn't claim "ownership" of a name for a function it doesn't want anymore (assuming a "here" already exists in the user's namespace)

title: A function to get the time component of a date-time
description:
A partner to the lubridate::date() function, which returns the H:M:S time component of a date-time. 

In the lubridate cheat sheet there is an example for date():

> **2018-01-31** 11:59:59 - date(x) Date component. date(dt)

I propose the need for a similar function on the time side:

> 2018-01-31 **11:59:59** - get_time(x) Time component. get_time(dt)

My function:
```
get_time <- function(t = now()) {
  strftime((t), format="%H:%M:%S", tz = tz(t)) 
}
```

title: period() not accepting vector input
description:
Example:
```
months(c(0,3)) # this works
# [1] "0S"             "3m 0d 0H 0M 0S"

period(num = 0, units = "month") # this works
# [1] "0S"

period(num = 3, units = "month") # this works
# [1] "3m 0d 0H 0M 0S"

period(num = c(0,3), units = "month") # oops, documentation clearly says it doesn't accept that
# Error in .period_from_num(num, units) : 
#   Arguments `num` and `units` must have same length

period(num = c(0,3), units = c("month","month")) # this is the bug
# Error: Invalid unit name: month

period(num = c(1,3), units = c("month","month")) # and it's not because of weird zero behavior
# Error: Invalid unit name: month
```

According to the documentation `period()` should accept "a numeric or character vector," and the shortcut call `months()` does, so I think this is a bug. Thanks for all you do supporting this awesome package!

title: Feature Request: as.ISO8601
description:
`as.ISO8601` methods would be useful for all the date, date/time, period, duration, and interval functions.

To make this as useful as possible, I think it would benefit to not use `as.character` and make a new `as.ISO8601` generic function with arguments:

* `x`: The object to convert
* `format`: This would depend on what is being represented:
    * With dates, it could be "ymd" (year month day), "ywd" (year week day), "yd" (year day in YYYY-DDD format), "y" (year only), "m" (month only), "md" (month day only)
    * With times, it could be "hms", "hm", or "h"
    * With date/times, it could be any pair of the options for dates and times separated by a "T" (default "ymdThms").  I chose "T" rather than something else to align with the expected output as defined in the ISO standard.
    * Periods would share the format specifier with date, times, or date/times.
* `include_tz`: if `NULL` (default), include/exclude the time zone from the date/time based on the input data.  If `FALSE`, exclude the time zone from the representation, and if `TRUE` include the time zone in the representation.  (It would be ignored if time zone does not apply to the output format.)
* `repeat`: (default: `NULL`) For intervals, repeating could be specified by setting to a non-NULL, positive integer or `Inf` for indefinite, future repeats.
* `repeat_start`: (default: `NULL`) For intervals, repeat start date/time.  (Must be a date, time, or date/time object type.)

(As initially discussed in #362)

title: Modify CODEOWNERS to stop auto-request for review
description:

title: Error when using weeks() in conjunction with Sys.time()
description:
I've just upgraded to lubridate 1.7.3 and am thrown an error when using `weeks()` in conjunction with `Sys.time()`:
```
Sys.time() - weeks(2)
Error in (function (dt, year, month, yday, mday, wday, hour, minute, second,  : 
  Invalid timezone of input vector: ""
```

If I wrap `Sys.time()` in `as_datetime()`, it works (but the timezone is shifted to UTC, which is no problem for my specific case but may be unexpected). 
```
as_datetime(Sys.time()) - weeks(2)
```

The error is also thrown when using `Sys.time()` in conjunction with similar function to `weeks()` (e.g. `months()`), so this may be a feature. In lubridate versions prior to 1.7.3 that I have used, `Sys.time() - weeks(2)` always worked. 
I think the right solution would be to assume timezone is UTC if timezone is not set (i.e. `tz(x) == ""`), and warn the user about this.

Warning message:
All formats failed to parse. No formats found. 
```
Expected result: last five dates correctly parsed.

title: Strange behavior of the timezones with unnest()
description:
(Feel free to tell me if this issue is more appropriate for `tidyr` than `lubridate`)

The behavior of `unnest()` regarding the timezones seems strange to me.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

Sys.getenv("TZ")
#[1] "Europe/Paris"

reprex_unnest <- tribble(
  ~datetime, ~locale,
  "2018-03-08 01:00:00",   "America/Argentina/Buenos_Aires",
  "2018-03-08 01:00:00",   "Europe/Kiev",
  "2018-03-08 01:00:00",   "UTC"
) %>%
  mutate(datetime = ymd_hms(datetime, tz = "UTC")
         , datetime_locale = map2(datetime, locale, ~ with_tz(.x, tzone = .y) ))%>%
  unnest(datetime_locale) %>% 
  mutate(tz_datetime = tz(datetime)
         , tz_datetime_locale = tz(datetime_locale))

reprex_unnest

# Source: local data frame [3 x 3]
# Groups: <by row>
# 
# # A tibble: 3 x 3
#   datetime            locale        datetime_locale     tz_datetime tz_datetime_locale
#   <dttm>              <chr>         <dttm>              <chr>       <chr>            
# 1 2018-03-08 01:00:00 America/Arge… 2018-03-08 01:00:00 UTC         UTC
# 2 2018-03-08 01:00:00 Europe/Kiev   2018-03-08 01:00:00 UTC         UTC
# 3 2018-03-08 01:00:00 UTC           2018-03-08 01:00:00 UTC         UTC
```

It seems `with_tz` wasn't applied

``` r
reprex_no_unnest <- tribble(
  ~datetime, ~locale,
  "2018-03-08 01:00:00",   "America/Argentina/Buenos_Aires",
  "2018-03-08 01:00:00",   "Europe/Kiev",
  "2018-03-08 01:00:00",   "UTC"
) %>%
  mutate(datetime = ymd_hms(datetime, tz = "UTC")) %>% 
  mutate(datetime_locale = map2(datetime, locale, ~ with_tz(.x, tzone = .y) ))

str(reprex_no_unnest)

# Classes ‘tbl_df’, ‘tbl’ and 'data.frame':	3 obs. of  3 variables:
#  $ datetime       : POSIXct, format: "2018-03-08 01:00:00" ...
#  $ locale         : chr  "America/Argentina/Buenos_Aires" "Europe/Kiev" "UTC"
#  $ datetime_locale:List of 3
#   ..$ : POSIXct, format: "2018-03-07 22:00:00"
#   ..$ : POSIXct, format: "2018-03-08 03:00:00"
#   ..$ : POSIXct, format: "2018-03-08 01:00:00"
```
But behind the scenes, `with_tz` actually is applied and returns the expected result.

I guess the issue boils down to this

``` r
tz(reprex$datetime_locale[1])
#[1] "UTC"
tz(reprex$datetime_locale[[1]])
#[1] "America/Argentina/Buenos_Aires"
tz(reprex$datetime_locale[[2]])
#[1] "Europe/Kiev"
```

The `tz` of the list column is actually UTC, and I guess it takes priority over the `tz` of each element.
It this an expected `R` behavior ?
Did I miss anything ?

title: Feature request/clarification: %within% for vectors of intervals
description:
%within% works wonderfully for the stated use case: a %within% b, 
where a is a date/datetime, and b is an single interval. 

But sometimes the user has a vector of intervals, even an unknown number of intervals, and the question  is whether is: a %within% B, where B is a vector of intervals (b1, b2, b3...)

Example:given a set of reward blackout dates for a frequent-flyer program, can I book a flight that leaves at a particular time? 

A very good solution is found here:
# thanks to:https://stackoverflow.com/questions/28682816/match-dates-against-date-intervals-holiday-periods-in-multiple-years

If we assume that df$datetimes holds the flight times , and blackouts$interval holds the blackout intervals we wish to include/exclude, with one record per blackout period:

apply(sapply(df$datetime, function(x) x %within% blackouts$interval),2,any)

works just fine, but its a bit "ugly" in that way that R can be ugly. 

So, two suggestions: 1) make explicit within the  %within% documentation that %within%t does not work across a vector of intervals 2) perhaps offer a nice purr-ized example of the above for this specific and I suspect common situation.

As always, thanks, thanks and thanks again for the tidyverse!

title: Feature request: a function to return both year and month, something like quarter()
description:
For multi-year boxplots stratified by quarter, the function lubridate::quarter(x, with_year=TRUE) function works wonderfully. quarter() does this by returning a numeric, e.g 2017.1, 2017.2 which strikes me as not exactly "true", but be that as it may, I often find myself using the construct:

geom_boxplot(aes(x=x, y=y, group=as.factor(quarter(x, with_year=TRUE))))

However, when monthly boxplots are required across multiple years I find myself constructing various, never-quite-satisfactory, hacked variants of quarter.  My feature request is for a lubridate function that  returns both the year and month in a single result.

It might be that this is part of month(), or perhaps it needs to be a separate function.

The central challenge is what should be returned?  I suspect a string with values something like:
"YEAR-MONTH", where month has a  leading zero for January to September., e.g. "2017-09".
I think this suggestion conforms with ISO 8601.

However, this suggestion of returning a string would be at odds with  quarter()'s returning of a real (as discussed above). 

A welcome alternative/supplementary suggestion would be to revise month() revised so that it can return not only a numeric or an abbreviation (which are existing features) but also a zero-padded string representing the month number.

Many thanks,

R

title: GPLv2 and ASL are incompatible
description:
The `DESCRIPTION` file says lubridate is GPL-2 and the description notes that some code from cctz is ASL 2.0. However, these two licenses are incompatible, e.g., see [this table](https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/Licensing:Main#Good_Licenses) or [Apache's own notes](https://www.apache.org/licenses/GPL-compatibility.html):
> the FSF has never considered the Apache License to be compatible with GPL version 2

ASL 2.0 _is_ compatible with GPLv3 so if lubridate were under that license, things would be fine (and the combined work would be GPLv3.) The files that say GPL2 _or later_ can be re-licensed no problem. There are other .c files that don't contain a license header and theoretically one needs consent from all contributors to change those licenses. However, looking at the files in GitHub only shows a single contributor so this may be a bit simpler.

cc @dpocock who wrote #383 because this is presumably also a problem for Debian packaging as well.

title: Intervals change when sorting data frame with dplyr::arrange
description:
Interval objects in a data frame / tibble column get "jumbled" when the data frame is being sorted with `dplyr::arrange`. I hope I'm not reading the documentation wrong, but I don't see why the Intervals should be affected in any way when sorting -- particularly in such a strange and unpredictable way.

library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)

# I'm using a tibble here, but I get the same issue with data.frame

n = 3
df <- tibble( 
  x = seq(n),
  t1 = today() - duration(sample(n), "days"),
  t2 = today() + duration(sample(n), "days"),
  p = interval(t1, t2))

# looks as expected
df %>% head()

# # A tibble: 4 × 4
#       x         t1         t2                              p
#   <int>     <date>     <date>                 <S4: Interval>

df %>% arrange(t1) %>% head()

# # A tibble: 4 × 4
#       x         t1         t2                              p
#   <int>     <date>     <date>                 <S4: Interval>

df %>% arrange(t2) %>% head()

# # A tibble: 4 × 4
#       x         t1         t2                              p
#   <int>     <date>     <date>                 <S4: Interval>
# 1     1 2017-02-07 2017-02-09 2017-02-07 UTC--2017-02-09 UTC
# 2     4 2017-02-06 2017-02-10 2017-02-05 UTC--2017-02-09 UTC
# 3     2 2017-02-05 2017-02-11 2017-02-04 UTC--2017-02-10 UTC
# 4     3 2017-02-04 2017-02-12 2017-02-06 UTC--2017-02-14 UTC

df %>% arrange(p) %>% head()

# # A tibble: 4 × 4

#   <int>     <date>     <date>                 <S4: Interval>

df %>% arrange(-x) %>% head()

# # A tibble: 4 × 4
#      x         t1         t2                              p
#  <int>     <date>     <date>                 <S4: Interval>
# 1     4 2017-02-06 2017-02-10 2017-02-07 UTC--2017-02-11 UTC
# 2     3 2017-02-04 2017-02-12 2017-02-05 UTC--2017-02-13 UTC
# 3     2 2017-02-05 2017-02-11 2017-02-04 UTC--2017-02-10 UTC

# if we keep t1 the same for all rows and sort by t2 it works as expected

df %>% 
  mutate(t1 = today(), p = interval(t1, t2)) %>% 
  arrange(t2) %>% 
  head()

# # A tibble: 4 × 4

# However, if t2 is fixed and we sort by t1, the problem occurs

title: ceiling_date rounding by day on DST change rounds to 23:00
description:
Apologies if this is a repeated issue, this seems slightly different from other DST bugs I saw reported.

``` r
library(lubridate)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'lubridate'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     date
x <- ymd_hms("2017-11-05 23:59:03", tz = 'America/New_York')
x
#> [1] "2017-11-05 23:59:03 EST"

ceiling_date(x, 'day')
#> [1] "2017-11-05 23:00:00 EST"
```

The issue arises in [round.r line 253](https://github.com/tidyverse/lubridate/blob/master/R/round.r#L253) when a "days" worth of seconds is added to `2017-11-05`.

Because of DST ending, 2017-11-05 has 25 hours but `ceiling_date(x, 'day')` only adds `86400` seconds (24 hours).

```r
y <- floor_date(x, 'day')
# Not what I expected, but accurate
y + 86400  
#> [1] "2017-11-05 23:00:00 EST"

# What I expected, seems accurate
y + days(1)
#> [1] "2017-11-06 EST"

# What I expected, but not accurate?
y + hours(24)
#> [1] "2017-11-06 EST"

# Hacky work-around
floor_date(x, 'day') + days(1)
#> [1] "2017-11-06 EST"


# Same for 2016, 2015...
ceiling_date(ymd_hm('2016-11-06 23:59', tz = 'America/New_York'), 'day')
#> [1] "2016-11-06 23:00:00 EST"
ceiling_date(ymd_hm('2015-11-01 23:59', tz = 'America/New_York'), 'day')
#> [1] "2015-11-01 23:00:00 EST"

# DST is overrated ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
```

title: Make duration() parse YouTube duration values
description:
```
> duration("11M22S")
[1] "682s (~11.37 minutes)"
```
is correct

```
> duration("PT11M22S")
[1] NA
```
is not.

The latter is the format used by YouTube for video duration, and is a valid notation option per the [ISO 8601 spec on durations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Durations).

More info on the YT duration format: look for `contentDetails.duration` on [this page](https://developers.google.com/youtube/v3/docs/videos).

title: Issue with Lubridate 1.7.0 and "America/Chicago"
description:
After updating to v1.7.0 it seems that `lubridate` no longer considers `"America/Chicago"` a time zone yet multiple other CST time zones are still recognized.

```
> ISOdatetime(2016, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, tz = "America/Chicago") - lubridate::years(1)
Error in (function (dt, year, month, yday, mday, wday, hour, minute, second,  : 
  Invalid timezone of input vector: "America/Chicago"
> ISOdatetime(2016, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, tz = "Canada/Central") - lubridate::years(1)
[1] "2015-01-01 CST"
> ISOdatetime(2016, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, tz = "US/Central") - lubridate::years(1)
[1] "2015-01-01 CST"
```

R version 3.4.1 (2017-06-30)

title: `with_tz()` warns about invalid timezones, but returns them correctly anyway
description:
This is a problem I've noticed on Windows only (not my Ubuntu machine). The warnings are also popping up in the AppVeyor tests (but not on Travis CI for Ubuntu and Mac). 

I *think* it's only in lubridate v0.7.0 (related to c10c8cfff6a8d86e58c5865c1fb1c93463be647e) but I had problems trying to install v0.6.0 to double check. 

`with_tz()` warns about invalid timezones, but returns them correctly anyway...

```
> Sys.time()
[1] "2017-11-02 00:17:10 AST"

> lubridate::with_tz(Sys.time(), "UTC")
[1] "2017-11-02 04:17:26"

> lubridate::with_tz(Sys.time(), "America/Vancouver")
[1] "2017-11-01 21:17:28 PDT"
Warning message:
In lubridate::with_tz(Sys.time(), "America/Vancouver") :
  Unrecognized time zone 'America/Vancouver'

> lubridate::with_tz(Sys.time(), "Etc/GMT+8")
[1] "2017-11-01 20:18:25 -08"
Warning message:
In lubridate::with_tz(Sys.time(), "Etc/GMT+8") :
  Unrecognized time zone 'Etc/GMT+8'
```

If I try a non-legitimate name I get a second warning message (and UTC):

```
> lubridate::with_tz(Sys.time(), "America/Van")
[1] "2017-11-02 04:41:31 GMT"
Warning messages:
1: In lubridate::with_tz(Sys.time(), "America/Van") :
  Unrecognized time zone 'America/Van'
2: In as.POSIXlt.POSIXct(x, tz) : unknown timezone "America/Van"
```

The first two are both legitimate timezones (i.e. they're in OlsonNames())

```
> OlsonNames()[OlsonNames() == "America/Vancouver"]
[1] "America/Vancouver"

> OlsonNames()[OlsonNames() == "Etc/GMT+8"]
[1] "Etc/GMT+8"

> OlsonNames()[OlsonNames() == "America/Van"]
character(0)
```

title: Issue with as_date reading a character with date and time
description:
With version 1.7.0 the as_date function does not convert a character with a date and time to a date, instead it returns NA with a warning.  The expected value to be returned was a date with the time portion dropped.  In version 1.6.0, the function converted the character to a date.
``` r
# See if as_date works with current version of lubridate to convert a character string with time
install.packages("lubridate")
#> (as 'lib' is unspecified)

lubridate::as_date("2017-10-31 06:00:00")
#> Warning: All formats failed to parse. No formats found.
#> [1] NA
packageVersion("lubridate")
#> [1] '1.7.0'
# See if as_date works with version 1.6 of lubridate to convert a character string with time
library(devtools)
install_version("lubridate", version = "1.6.0", repos = "http://cran.us.r-project.org")
#> 
lubridate::as_date("2017-10-31 06:00:00")
#> [1] "2017-10-31"

#> [1] '1.6.0'
```

title: with_tz is not vectorized over `tzone` parameter
description:
The `with_tz()` function is not vectorized over the tzname argument. Minimal example:

```r
t1 <- lubridate::now()

lubridate::with_tz(t1, "UTC")
# [1] "2017-10-24 12:29:27 UTC"

lubridate::with_tz(rep(t1, 2), "UTC")
# [1] "2017-10-24 12:29:27 UTC" "2017-10-24 12:29:27 UTC"

lubridate::with_tz(rep(t1, 2), rep("UTC", 2))
# Error in as.POSIXlt.POSIXct(x, tz) : invalid 'tz' value 
```

This creates problems when calling `with_tz()` from within `mutate()` like this:
```r
data.frame(t1 = rep(t1), tz = rep("UTC")) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(t2 = lubridate::with_tz(t1, tz))
#  Error in as.POSIXlt.POSIXct(x, tz) : invalid 'tz' value 
```

title: Time zone stripped when vectorizing date created with ymd_hms() on Linux
description:
When we simply run the command, `ymd_hms('2017-10-23T18:30:00-06:00', tz = 'America/Denver')`, the results are consistent. However, when we vectorize
 `c(ymd_hms('2017-10-23T18:30:00-06:00', tz = 'America/Denver'))`, we obtain different results on Mac and on Linux:

On Mac (R version 3.4.0):
```
> c(ymd_hms('2017-10-23T18:30:00-06:00', tz = 'America/Denver'))
Date in ISO8601 format; converting timezone from UTC to "America/Denver".
[1] "2017-10-24 00:30:00 UTC"
```
On Linux VM (R version 3.3.3):
```
> c(ymd_hms('2017-10-23T18:30:00-06:00', tz = 'America/Denver'))
Date in ISO8601 format; converting timezone from UTC to "America/Denver".
[1] "2017-10-23 18:30:00 MDT"
```

It appears that when the date is vectorized on the Linux VM, the time zone is stripped and the date is automatically converted to UTC.  

Both the Mac and the Linux VM are running lubridate version 1.6.0.

title: duration() interpreting 0[units] as 1[units] when argument is single string
description:
I only tested this for hours and minutes (as you can see below), so I'm not sure how general the issue is.
I'm also not sure if indeed it is an issue or just outside the intended use of the function (or if I'm doing something stupid).

```
> duration("2d 0H 0M 1s")
[1] "176461s (~2.04 days)"
> as.numeric(duration("2d 0H 0M 1s"))
[1] 176461
> 2*24*3600 + 1
[1] 172801
> 
> duration("2d 1s")
[1] "172801s (~2 days)"
> as.numeric(duration("2d 1s"))

title: Feature Request: Add a cutoff year to decide if 21th century or not
description:
Hello.

It would be nice to have a cutoff parameter for commands such as dmy().
It's quite common to deal with dates stored as 31-12-40 or 12/31/70 where the year is stored with just 2 digits. That's a bad way to do it but there are many databases like that.

If you just use lubruidate commands to convert that strings to dates the user can get unexpected results.
And what's more serious, it can even miss he is having a problem till is too late.

The user can transform the data by doing:

```
mydates <- dmy(mydates)
yyy <- year(mydates) %% 100  
year(mydates) <- ifelse(yyy > 20, 1900+yyy, 2000+yyy)

```
or

```
dmy(paste0(sub("\\d\\d$","",xxx) , ifelse( (tt <- 
   sub("\\d\\d-\\D\\D\\D-","",xxx)  ) > 20 ,paste0("19",tt),paste0("20",tt))))

```
But this would need to be modyfied depending on the exact formats the user has and wants, and it's prone to error and takes a lot of code for a simple task.

Could you please add a "cutoff" date parameter to lubridate functions to allow the user to just do `dmy(mydates, cutoff=20)` when he wants to consider numbers bellow 20 as 20xx and numbers above 20 as 19xx, please?

I think it should be easy because somewhere you already do it, you just need to expose that parameter to the user.
And I think it would be very useful.
I will also allow to easily use the same syntax across different libraries.

title: bug in hms function
Proposal for new func to calculate epiweek and epiyear
description:
The epiweek function takes a scalar x or vector x and returns the numeric epiweek for that date.
  
x can be entered as in any format recognized by lubridate's isoweek i.e., a date-time object. Must be a POSIXct, POSIXlt, Date, chron, yearmon, yearqtr, zoo, zooreg, timeDate, xts, its, ti, jul, timeSeries, or fts object
Here is the "definition" I've been working from (this defines both week and year).

The first epi week of the year ends, by definition, on the first Saturday of January, as long as it falls at least four days into the month. Each epi week begins on a Sunday and ends on a Saturday.

This can be achieved by simple change to isoweek and isoyear.

epiweek is based on isoweek from lubridate. The difference is in dn, where we add +6 here and +4 in isoweek because here we want to know where first *Sat* falls rather than first *Thurs* as in isoweek.


epiweek <- function(x)
{
  require(lubridate)
  xdate <- make_datetime(year(x), month(x), day(x))
  dn <- 1 + (wday(xdate) + 6)%%7
  nth <- xdate + ddays(4 - dn)
  jan1 <- make_datetime(year(nth), 1, 1)
  1L + as.integer(difftime(nth, jan1, units = "days")) %/% 7L
}


epiyear <- function(x)
{
  require(lubridate)
  xdate <- make_datetime(year(x), month(x), day(x))
  dn <- 1 + (wday(xdate) + 6)%%7
  nth <- xdate + ddays(4 - dn)
  year(nth)
}

title: Inconsistent date parsing when year has 2 or 4 digits and the monts is written in lower case
description:
Hi all, 
This issue maybe be related to #425 .

The date-parsing behavior of `parse_date_time()` is inconsistent depending on whether one or more dates are given, and if it is a mixture of 2- or 4-digit year. For 2-digit year, for instace "16.dec.25", the result is "2016-12-25". However, when the same date is parsed with a date of 4-digit year, for instance "2016.dec.25", it results in "16-12-25".

Examples
```
parse_date_time(c("16.dec.25"), orders = "ymd")    # "2016-12-25"
parse_date_time(c("2016.dec.25", "16.dec.25"), orders = "ymd")    # "2016-12-25" "16-12-25"
parse_date_time(c("16.dec.25", "16.dec.25"), orders = "ymd")    # "2016-12-25" "2016-12-25"

parse_date_time(c("2016.Dec.25", "16.Dec.25"), orders = "ymd")    # "2016-12-25" "2016-12-25"

title: Updating on both years and ydays leads to wrong results with leap years
description:
```
> update(ymd("15-05-03"), year = 2016, yday = 1)
[1] "2016-01-02 UTC"
```

This has to do with the computation of the days differential in `update.POSIXlt` which is done on the current year. I don't see how to fix this without affecting performance so I am adding a warning for now.

A workaround is to update on month and month day, or do two consecutive updates:

```
> update(ymd("15-05-03"), year = 2016, month = 1, day = 1)
[1] "2016-01-01 UTC"
> update(update(ymd("15-05-03"), year = 2016), yday = 1)
[1] "2016-01-01 UTC"
> 
```

title: inconsistent arithmetic in subtraction of hms() / periods
description:
Hi!

When I try to subtract a period object created by hms() from another I find it gives faulty results. Searching to see if I had misused period subtraction I found this post on [Stackoverflow](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/11298327/in-r-use-lubridate-to-convert-hms-objects-into-seconds) by Dirk Eddelbuettel which seems to suggest that subtraction of periods is legit.

Example of expected correct result when the subtrahend is less than the minuend:
```
> hms("12:34:45") - hms("10:10:00")
[1] "2H 24M 45S"
```
Unclear result when subtracting and the minute or second subtrahend part is greater than the minuend:  
```
> hms("20:03:00") - hms("19:55:00")
[1] "1H -52M 0S"
```
```
> hms("20:03:00") - hms("19:55:00") + hms("-01:52:00")
[1] "0S"
```
while "correct" it would be much nicer if the result of the subtraction as with addition is expressed as
```
[1] "8M 0S"
```
another example
```
> hms("12:34:45") - hms("11:50:00")
[1] "1H -16M 45S"
```
where you would expect
`[1] "44M 45S"`

Perhaps it would be easier to understand and use if there was a default automatic rollover from seconds -> minutes -> hours when doing additions and subtractions like when you construct a period using hms(...,roll=TRUE).


Here is another situation but somewhat contrived. Since lubridate can create hms/period objects with a greater amount of HH:MM:SS than the conventional 23:59:59 another subtraction inconsistency as compared to addition arises:

Addition is ok:
```
> hms("13:15:45") + hms("14:25:45")
[1] "27H 40M 90S"
```
and then the overflow seconds can be corrected by adding another hms() call, although somewhat inconveniently in comparison to the otherwise sleek syntax in lubridate: 
```
hms(hms("13:15:45") + hms("14:25:45"),roll=TRUE)
"27H 41M 30S"
```
with subtraction:
```
> hms("13:15:15") - hms("14:25:95")
[1] "-1H -10M -80S"
> hms(hms("13:15:15") - hms("14:25:95"),roll=TRUE)
[1] NA
Warning message:
In .parse_hms(..., order = "HMS", quiet = quiet) :
  Some strings failed to parse
```


In any case, I would like to thank you so much for lubridate which has made working with dates and times so much easier!

title: `as_datetime()` doesn’t really respect `tz` for character objects
description:
The `as_datetime()` function doesn’t work as expected for *character* objects.

**Expected behaviour**: The datetime string should be interpreted as a datetime in the chosen time zone `tz` (UTC by default).

**Actual behaviour**: The datetime string is interpreted as a datetime in the *current* time zone (including any DST-specific stuff) and *then* converted to the `tz` timezone.

Example (as run in the `CET` time zone):

    > as_datetime("2015-01-04 03:10:00")
    [1] "2015-01-04 02:10:00 UTC"
    > as_datetime("2015-01-04 03:10:00", tz="UTC")
    [1] "2015-01-04 02:10:00 UTC"

Note that the time part is an hour off. Expected result:

    [1] "2015-01-04 03:10:00 UTC"

title: Make cut method for instants
description:
A cut function would be sensible for any date-time class that measures an instant, such as POSIXct, POSIXlt, Date, and well all of them except difftime and the ones we've created: period, duration, interval.

As long as the date-times of x are measured in classes we've made compatible with lubridate, we can turn the range into an interval object. From there we could turn it into a duration to do an exactly spaced cut, or a period to cut by units such as days, hours, etc. Once we do the cut, we can assign each x its marker variable and let it keep its orginal date-time stamp in whatever class it came in.

}

 So this data:

Rather than this:

title: Help for confusing `strftime()`?
description:
The built-in `base::strftime` function has some dangerous pitfalls around timezones:

```
> d <- strptime('2005-03-26 12:00:01', "%F %T", tz='America/New_York')
> d
[1] "2005-03-26 12:00:01 EST"
> tz(d)
[1] "America/New_York"

# Bad: wrong offset shown - this is actually the wrong instant
> strftime(d, "%F %T%z")
[1] "2005-03-26 12:00:01+0000"

# Bad: timezone is lost - this is the right instant but in the wrong timezone
> strftime(as.POSIXct(d), "%F %T%z")
[1] "2005-03-26 17:00:01+0000"
> strftime(as.POSIXct(d, tz=tz(d)), "%F %T%z")
[1] "2005-03-26 17:00:01+0000"

# Good
> strftime(as.POSIXct(d), "%F %T%z", tz=tz(d))
[1] "2005-03-26 12:00:01-0500"
```

Since `lubridate`'s niche is (at least in part) to help people avoid these pitfalls with alternative functions like `as_posixct()`, have you thought about adding a helper function people could use instead of `strftime()` that would have safer default semantics?

title: `duration` ignores class of first argument
description:
See [:link: Stack Overflow question](http://stackoverflow.com/q/39163160/1968).

In a nutshell, the following code

``` r
time = now()
five_sec = interval(time, time + 5)
duration(five_sec)
# [1] "5s"
duration(five_sec, units = 'days')
# [1] "432000s (~5 days)"
```

Yields an unexpected output for the last line because the class of `five_sec` is ignored, and its unit is overridden to be interpreted as `days`. This makes sense for a unitless `num` argument — but `five_sec` isn’t unitless by virtue of being an `Interval`.

The expected behaviour is that this should be disallowed — i.e. throw an error, or at least signal a stern warning that the interval’s unit is being ignored.

At first I thought it could be `data.tabl` trying to update the huge object at the same time, so I wrote it separately instead of creating column in place. Turned out it is not the case. Instead `as.POSIXct` didn't have this problem. See the comparison below with the helper methods from package `pryr`:

`as.POSIXct` works without more memory usage

```
> memory.size()
[1] 9198.51
> ptm = proc.time()
> mem_change(as.POSIXct(nyc311$`Created Date`, format = "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p"))
-5.94 kB
> proc.time() - ptm
   user  system elapsed 
 248.24    1.33  278.78 
```

`parse_date_time` didn't finish even with more memory available (I set memory limit to 16G):

```
> memory.size()
[1] 5716.69
> ptm = proc.time()
> mem_change(nyc311[, parse_date_time(`Created Date`, tz = "America/New_York", "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p")])
Error: evaluation nested too deeply: infinite recursion / options(expressions=)?
Error during wrapup: evaluation nested too deeply: infinite recursion / options(expressions=)?
> proc.time() - ptm
   user  system elapsed 
 256.79    2.10  303.72 
```

It doesn't help if I wrote separately without data.table syntax:

```
> memory.size()
[1] 8135.76
> ptm = proc.time()
> mem_change(parse_date_time(nyc311$`Created Date`, tz = "America/New_York", "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p"))
Error: evaluation nested too deeply: infinite recursion / options(expressions=)?
Error during wrapup: evaluation nested too deeply: infinite recursion / options(expressions=)?
> proc.time() - ptm
   user  system elapsed 
 259.58    2.48  279.07 
```

I also didn't see performance improvement I expected on `parse_date_time`. I knew `parse_date_time2` and `fast_strptime` probably will be much faster but I cannot use them since I need the `I` and `p` format to recognize AM/PM string.

title: ymd() returns Date instead of POSIXct - please keep API stable (backward compatible)
description:
Dear lubridate team,

the most recent update of lubridate to version 1.5.6 introduced a problem to ymd() by implementing the feature request [ Should ymd() and similar return a date? #391 ](https://github.com/hadley/lubridate/issues/391).

Before:

```
> class(ymd("1980-01-01"))
[1] "POSIXct" "POSIXt"
```

After update to lubridate 1.5.6:

```
> class(ymd("1980-01-01"))
[1] "Date"
```

**Therefore existing code breaks if it relies on POSIXct as class of the return value.**

Can you please fix this problem by
1. switching back to POSIXct or
2. introduce a new function like "ymd_POSIXct" that behaves like before for a simple migration of existing code by search&replace or
3. adding an additional parameter to ymd() specifying the return type or
4. add a new R option that can be configured globally to switch this behaviour.

**Generally I would suggest to not change the signature of a function any-more if it has been released.**

You could add a new function instead (e. g. "ymd2") like you can observe it sometimes in the Windows C API.

PS: The documentation is also wrong partially (still mentions POSIXct as return type): I will file a separate issue for this

[1] 0.0001138434 0.0002276867
```

The times above are a fixed hour apart however the decimal_date function ignores the tz information. Not sure this is intentional but it doesn't seem necessary unless I'm missing something.

I've fixed the issue in my fork and and wrote a couple tests. All tests in test-decimal-date passed. I'll issue a pull request shortly.

title: Convert Period to numeric
description:
I couldn't find the right way to do it, but it seems hard to convert Period elements to numeric.
This is the expected behavior (`as.numeric` on `difftime`)

``` r
as.numeric(as.difftime("24:00:00"), "hours")
# [1] 24
as.numeric(as.difftime("24:00:00"), "mins")
# [1] 1440

```

However Period objects only return the `unit`part of the Period, like components getters (`second`, `minute`, ... )

``` r
as.numeric(period(24, "hours"), "mins")
# [1] 0  # This is unexpected to me, I believe it's an error
as.numeric(period(24, "hours") + period(10, "minutes"), "mins")
# [1] 10
as.numeric(period(24, "hours"), "hours")
# [1] 24
```

The trick I found was to convert to duration, but I get a warning when converting `Period` to `duration`.

``` r
as.numeric(as.duration(period(10, "minutes")), "mins")
# estimate only: convert periods to intervals for accuracy
# [1] 10
as.numeric(as.duration(period(10, "minutes")), "hours")
# estimate only: convert periods to intervals for accuracy
# [1] 0.1666667
```

title: Inconsistent date parsing when year has 2 or 4 digits
description:
The date-parsing behavior of `mdy`, `dmy`, and `ymd` is inconsistent depending on whether one or more dates are given.

If a date with a 2-digit year is parsed, say `6/25/15`, it is parsed with year `2015`. However, the same date is parsed with year `0015` if included within a vector that includes a date with a 4-digit year.

``` r
d1 <- "6/25/15"
d2 <- "6/25/2015"
d3 <- c("6/25/15", "6/25/2015")

lubridate::mdy(d1)  # [1] "2015-06-25"
lubridate::mdy(d2)  # [1] "2015-06-25"
lubridate::mdy(d3)  # [1] "0015-06-25" "2015-06-25"
```

Similar behavior occurs for `dmy` and `ymd`:

``` r
d4 <- "25/6/15"
d5 <- "25/6/2015"
d6 <- c("25/6/15", "25/6/2015")

lubridate::dmy(d4)  # [1] "2015-06-25"
lubridate::dmy(d5)  # [1] "2015-06-25"
lubridate::dmy(d6)  # [1] "0015-06-25" "2015-06-25"

d7 <- "15/6/25"
d8 <- "2015/6/25"
d9 <- c("15/6/25", "2015/6/25")

lubridate::ymd(d7)  # [1] "2015-06-25"
lubridate::ymd(d8)  # [1] "2015-06-25"
lubridate::ymd(d9)  # [1] "0015-06-25" "2015-06-25"
```

the most recent update of lubridate to version 1.5.6 introduced a problem to ymd() by implementing the feature request [ Should ymd() and similar return a date? #391 ](https://github.com/hadley/lubridate/issues/391).

 `ceiling_date(dmy("01.04.2016"), 'month')` returns `2016-04-01`. 

This means that the function `last_day()` provided on the [lubridate vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lubridate/vignettes/lubridate.html) is not working when the date is the first of a month:

`
last_day <- function(date) {
        ceiling_date(date, "month") - days(1)
}
`

`last_day(dmy("02.04.2016"))` returns `2016-04-30` but `last_day(dmy("01.04.2016"))` returns `2016-03-31`

title: Use another locale parse_date_time()?
description:
[Question on SO](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/34375758/date-recognition-fails-with-strptime-and-parse-date-time-dont-know-why).

I had an odd error about:

```
parse_date_time("31/Dec/2012:06:20:10", orders = "dbYHMS")
parse_date_time("01/May/2013:00:01:37", orders = "dbYHMS")
```

The first works fine, the second returns NA. I could not find the problem. Eventually, I tried all the months and noticed that "Oct" also does not work. Then I realized what the problem was: it uses the system locale on default which is Danish, not English (for me). The abbreviations for these two months are different ("May" vs. "Maj", and "Oct" vs. "Okt"), but the rest just happen to match the English ones.

I searched and cannot find a way to change the locale for parsing times. Is it possible? I tried:

```

[1] "LC_COLLATE=Danish_Denmark.1252;LC_CTYPE=Danish_Denmark.1252;LC_MONETARY=Danish_Denmark.1252;LC_NUMERIC=C;LC_TIME=Danish_Denmark.1252"
```

Which seems to show that no other locales are available. Not sure how to proceed from here.

As a workaround, one can replace the month names first, but it is not a good solution.

title: Allow negative offsets in `hms` parsers
Add make_date() feature for converting date-times into dates
description:
I propose adding a convenience function `make_date()` for converting date-times to dates. One might by tempted to use `as.Date()`, and this works in many cases, but with the default options it gives surprising results in a few cases. Example:

  x1 = as.POSIXct("2010-08-03 00:59:59.23")
  x2 = as.POSIXct("2010-08-03 00:59:59.23", tz="Europe/London")
  x3 = as.POSIXct("2010-11-03 00:59:59.23")
  x4 = as.POSIXct("2010-11-03 00:59:59.23", tz="Europe/London")

The naïve user might expect `as.Date()` to return the 3rd of the month (August/November) for all of `x1`–`x4`. However, on my system (a `Europe/Oslo` timezone), I get:

```
> as.Date(x1)
[1] "2010-08-02"
> as.Date(x2)
[1] "2010-08-02"
> as.Date(x3)
[1] "2010-11-02"
> as.Date(x4)
[1] "2010-11-03"
```

It’s even more surprising if you have already used `floor_date(x, "day")` on the objects to remove the ‘time’ part.

The way to get the correct date (`Date`) corresponding to a date-time is either `as.Date(format(x, "%Y-%m-%d"))` or (preferably) `as.Date(x, tz=attr(x, "tzone"))`:

```
> as.Date(x1, tz=attr(x1, "tzone"))
[1] "2010-08-03"
> as.Date(x2, tz=attr(x2, "tzone"))
[1] "2010-08-03"
> as.Date(x3, tz=attr(x3, "tzone"))
[1] "2010-11-03"
> as.Date(x4, tz=attr(x4, "tzone"))
[1] "2010-11-03"
```

So I propose adding such a convenience function `make_date()` to `lubridate`, that would run

```
as.Date(x, tz=attr(x, "tzone"))
```

for `POSIXct` and `POSIXlt` objects (and just return `x` for `Date()` objects).

I just based the name on the `make_difftime()` function; other names may better.

title: fast_strptime differs from strptime in regards to tz parameter
description:
It seems that fast_strptime considers the input string to be specified in GMT and uses its `tz` argument to bring the specified time relative to the timezone of the tz argument.

```
> "12/03/16 12:00" %>% strptime("%d/%m/%y %H:%M", tz="Europe/Zurich")
[1] "2016-03-12 12:00:00 CET"
```

versus

```
> "12/03/16 12:00" %>% fast_strptime("%d/%m/%y %H:%M", tz="Europe/Zurich")
[1] "2016-03-12 13:00:00 CET"
```

I am running R 3.2.3 and lubridate 1.5.0.

title: ceiling_date behavior (at boundary) is undocumented
description:
`ceiling_date` seems to give erroneous results.  Consider the following example:

```
library(lubridate)
packageVersion( 'lubridate')
# [1] 1.3.3

 Sys.setenv( TZ="UTC" )
 dt <- ymd( "20120930", "20121001", "20121002", "20121101" )
 floor_date( dt, "month" )
 # [1] "2012-09-01 UTC" "2012-10-01 UTC" "2012-10-01 UTC" "2012-11-01 UTC"
 ceiling_date( dt, "month" )
 # [1] "2012-10-01 UTC" "2012-10-01 UTC" "2012-11-01 UTC" "2012-11-01 UTC"
```

I expect the second result to be "2012-11-01 UTC", i.e. like the third.  This is consistently wrong as seen by the fourth argument.

The problem appears to be with the following expression in `ceiling_date`:
     `y <- floor_date(x - eseconds(1), unit)`

I don't believe that there is a reason to subtract a second.  Changing this to:
     `y <- floor_date( x, unit )` 

fixes the issue.

Also, I realize that the ship has probably sailed on this, but shouldn't the ceiling for a month be the last second in the month, e.g. `2012-10-31 12:59:59` rather than the first second of the following month?

title: with_tz to support dataframes?
description:
Could we consider adapting `with_tz()` (and possibly `force_tz()`) to accept dataframes as well as vectors?

This is a follow-on to hadley/readr#230.

The idea would be that if the first arg is a vector, `with_tz()` would behave as it does currently.

If the first arg is a dataframe, `with_tz()` would loop over all the time-columns of the dataframe, and call `with_tz()` on them.

If you like, I could work up a PR.

Thanks,

Ian

title: Both parse_date_time and as.POSIXct  cannot parse ""01/01/2010 00:00:01 AM"
description:
I want to create a date time object as cut off reference point for all date time after 2010. So I tried to create it like this:

```
> as.POSIXct("01/01/2010 00:00:01 AM", tz = "America/New_York", format = "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p")
[1] NA
```

`parse_date_time` have same result:

```
> parse_date_time("01/01/2010 00:00:01 AM", "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p",  tz = "America/New_York")
[1] NA
Warning message:
All formats failed to parse. No formats found. 
```

I found they can deal with the string without AM/PM:

```
> parse_date_time("01/01/2010 00:00:01", "%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S",  tz = "America/New_York")
[1] "2010-01-01 00:00:01 EST"
```

and if the hour is at least 1:

```
> parse_date_time("01/01/2010 01:00:01 AM", "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p",  tz = "America/New_York")
[1] "2010-01-01 01:00:01 EST"
```

Of course I can work around this by using the string without AM/PM or even ignore the time part only using date, but I felt the inconsistency here may implying some bugs.

title: as.period doesn't convert to specified time units if x is a vector

``` R
ints <- c(

)

`as.period` converts correctly to the specified time units if the variable is a scalar:

title: maintain attributes of intervals when using Reduce
description:

``` R
df <- data.frame(id=c(1, 2, 3),
             interval=c(
               new_interval(ymd("2001-01-01"), ymd("2002-01-01")),
               new_interval(ymd("2001-01-01"), ymd("2004-01-01")),
               new_interval(ymd("2001-02-01"), ymd("2002-01-01"))
               ))
df
#   id                       interval
#1  1 2001-01-01 UTC--2002-01-01 UTC
#2  2 2001-01-01 UTC--2004-01-01 UTC
#3  3 2001-02-01 UTC--2002-01-01 UTC

lubridate::union(lubridate::union(df$interval[1], df$interval[2]),
                 df$interval[3])
# [1] 2001-01-01 UTC--2004-01-01 UTC

Reduce(lubridate::union, df$interval )

The intervals objects seem to get converted to numeric too son (before applying the union).

title: How do you determine leap years?
description:
Hi Hadley,

I wonder how you determine internally what is a leap year?

When I was working on your early `readr` package, I educated myself on the topic because `readr` would not convert appropriately. Here is what I discovered:

> if (year is not exactly divisible by 4) then (it is a common year)
> else
> if (year is not exactly divisible by 100) then (it is a leap year)
> else
> if (year is not exactly divisible by 400) then (it is a common year)
> else (it is a leap year)

Hence 2000 is a leap year but 1900 is not for example. Does `lubridate` account for that?

Best,
-Aymeric

title: parse_date_time on dates with weekdays fails when weekday (a / A) is specified in order
description:
