```
dat <- c("Saturday 31 August 2013", "Sun 12 Jan 2014")

parse_date_time(x = dat, orders = c("a d b y"), locale = "eng")
# [1] NA NA
# Warning message:
# All formats failed to parse. No formats found. 

parse_date_time(x = dat, orders = c("A d b y"), locale = "eng")
# [1] NA NA
# Warning message:
# All formats failed to parse. No formats found. 

parse_date_time(x = dat, orders = c("d b y"), locale = "eng")
# [1] "2013-08-31 UTC" "2014-01-12 UTC"

lubridate_1.3.3
```

title: Intervals calculated in group_by are assigned wrong units for some values
description:
I have calculated an interval for my data based on grouped data in dplyr.  For each group I subtract max(dt) - min(dt), where dt is a POSIXct variable in my dataframe.  For 4 of my 5 groups, the result is between 1 and 2 days, but for the other group, the result is 10 hours.  When I look at the dataframe, however, the unit label for all rows is days (i.e. 1.25 days, 1.3 days, 1.1 days, 10 days, 1.9 days).  This is incorrect, because the value 10 is actually hours, not days.  I presume this has something to do with the fact that the interval calculations are happening independently within each group and therefore the units are decided independently, but there must be some requirement for the unit label to be the same for all values in a column?

I've included a minimal reproducible example:

```
library(lubridate)
library(dplyr)

structure(list(dt = structure(c(1426802400, 1426906800, 1426910400, 
1426946400, 1426946400, 1426950000, 1427086800, 1427090400, 1427198400
), tzone = "UTC", class = c("POSIXct", "POSIXt")), event_interval = structure(c(1L, 
1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 3L, 4L, 4L), .Label = c("1", "2", "3", "4"
), class = "factor")), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
), row.names = c(NA, -9L), .Names = c("dt", "event_interval"))

ex_df %>% group_by(event_interval) %>% summarize(time_int = max(dt) - min(dt))
```

title: isoweek() returns wrong week during summertime
description:
isoweek() returns wrong week during summertime

If format is POSIXct and tz  = "Europe/London", isoweek() will return wrong week when daylight saving time is active.
If tz =  "GMT"  isoweek() will return correct value even during summer time.

Se examples below:

```
isoweek(as.POSIXct("2015-04-27", tz = "Europe/London")) #Wrong week
isoweek(as.POSIXct("2015-04-27", tz = "GMT"))   #Correct week

isoweek(as.POSIXct("2015-01-15", tz = "Europe/London")) #Correct week
isoweek(as.POSIXct("2015-01-15", tz = "GMT")) #Correct week 
```

title: Adding 10 seconds to any date with 20:59:50 results in NA
description:
I encountered something odd today, which looks to me like a bug.  I had been running R 2.15.2 with lubridate_1.2.0, I can do the following normal thing:

> ymd_hms('2013-05-01 20:59:50')+seconds(10)
> [1] "2013-05-01 21:00:00 UTC"

However, with R 3.0.0 and lubridate_1.3.0, I get the following:

> ymd_hms('2013-05-01 20:59:50')+seconds(10)
> [1] NA

I get an NA for any date that I try as long as the timestamp is 20:59:50 and I add seconds(10).  Actually, it looks like I get an NA for any timestamp (like 20:59:30) and interval combo in seconds (like seconds(30)) that would have a resulting timestamp of 21:00:00.  If the interval is in minutes or hours, it works though:

> ymd_hms('2013-05-01 20:00:00')+hours(1)
> [1] "2013-05-01 21:00:00 UTC"
> ymd_hms('2013-05-01 20:50:00')+minutes(10)
> [1] "2013-05-01 21:00:00 UTC"

Any ideas?

Michelangelo

title: Isoweek() problem in European timezones
description:
Hi, it appears that there is a problem with the `isoweek()` function for European timezones.

For instance tomorrow, April 14th 2015, it is Tuesday of week 16 here in Copenhagen, Denmark, but `isoweek` says it is week 15:

``` r
> ymd_hms("2015-04-14 16:45:00", tz="Europe/Copenhagen")
[1] "2015-04-14 16:45:00 CEST"
> isoweek(ymd_hms("2015-04-14 16:45:00", tz="Europe/Copenhagen"))
[1] 15  # Wrong
```

For UTC, it correctly returns week 16:

``` r
> ymd_hms("2015-04-14 16:45:00", tz="UTC")
[1] "2015-04-14 16:45:00 UTC"
> isoweek(ymd_hms("2015-04-14 16:45:00", tz="UTC"))
[1] 16  # Correct
```

Note that CEST (Central European Summer Time) is UTC + 2, so this should not influence the week number on a Tuesday afternoon.

It does not work for CET either:

``` r
> ymd_hms("2015-04-14 16:45:00", tz="CET")
[1] "2015-04-14 16:45:00 CEST"
> isoweek(ymd_hms("2015-04-14 16:45:00", tz="CET"))
[1] 15  # Wrong
```

So this appears to be a bug in lubridate or in the general handling of timezones.

(I am using lubridate 1.3.3 with 32-bit R 3.1.3 in RStudio 0.98.1103 on 64-bit Windows 7 SP1.)

Best regards,
Johan

ps: Finding the `isoweek()` function in the first place took me actually quite a while, since I did not see it mentioned when I skimmed the `week()` documentation via `?week`. I suggest adding a "See also" section or an example mentioning `isoweek()` to the `week()` documentation to highlight its existence.

title: unique() for Interval?
description:
unique() doesn't appear to be defined for class Interval, yet it silently runs and produces results that (I think) don't make sense.

example:

``` R
foo <- Sys.time() + days(1:4)
ints <- rep(interval(head(foo, -1), tail(foo, -1)), 2)
## each interval is the same _duration_, and unique(ints) simply returns the unique durations (in seconds).
## would (reasonably) expect the 3 unique _intervals_, instead.
unique(ints)
## [1] 86400
```

title: NA when adding 60 seconds to date times with 59 minutes
description:
Adding seconds returns NAs when result has new hour and zero seconds

```
library(lubridate)
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 00:59:00") + seconds(60)
## [1] NA
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 01:59:00") + seconds(60)
## [1] NA
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 23:59:00") + seconds(60)
## [1] NA
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 00:59:05") + seconds(55)
## [1] NA
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 00:59:59") + seconds(1)
## [1] NA
```

Doing the equivalent with `minutes(1)` works

```
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 00:59:00") + minutes(1)
## [1] "2015-01-01 01:00:00 UTC"
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 01:59:00") + minutes(1)
## [1] "2015-01-01 02:00:00 UTC"
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 23:59:00") + minutes(1)
## [1] "2015-01-02 UTC"
```

NA only occurs when result has new hour and zero seconds

```
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 00:59:00") + seconds(59)
## [1] "2015-01-01 00:59:59 UTC"
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 00:59:00") + seconds(61)
## [1] "2015-01-01 01:00:01 UTC"
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 00:58:00") + seconds(60)
## [1] "2015-01-01 00:59:00 UTC" 
```

NA does not occur when adding more than 60 seconds to create new hour and zero seconds

```
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 00:58:59") + seconds(61)
## [1] "2015-01-01 01:00:00 UTC"
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 00:58:55") + seconds(65)
## [1] "2015-01-01 01:00:00 UTC"
ymd_hms("2015-01-01 23:58:00") + seconds(120)
## [1] "2015-01-02 UTC"
```

title: Shortcuts for parsing large vectors of time strings, where many are repeated/redundant/same.
description:
When I work with large time data on a structured time grid (i.e. readings from multiple sources, but with the same time stamp), and is delivered as a text file, I find that it is not efficient to simply parse the time stamp column directly, since it will have to run the parser tens of millions of times.

Instead, I find it faster to do what I call the "merge trick". Here is an example of the pattern:

``` R
# suppose long_data is a large time series data set with regularly spaced datetimes
timestamps <- data.frame(datetime_txt = unique(long_data$datetime)) # much shorter than long_data
timestamps$datetime <- lubridate::ymd_hms(timestamps$datetime_txt)

# now, I merge back the parsed timestamps onto long data
long_data <- merge(long_data, timestamps, by = "datetime") 
# often much faster than parsing, esp. when number of unique timestamps is much less than number of rows.
```

I feel like this is a common situation for many people. Is something similar to the "merge trick" built into lubridate (i.e. something that takes advantage of redundant timestamps). If you tried something like this:

``` r
same_ts <- rep("2015-01-01 00:00:00", 1e6)
y <- lubridate::ymd_hms(same_ts)
```

This still takes a significant amount of time, even though, you could get the same result doing this:

``` r
# this is still slow, i guess because of order of evaluation!
# y <- rep(lubridate::ymd_hms("2015-01-01 00:00:00"), 1e6)
one_ts <- lubridate::yms_hms("2015-01-01 00:00:00")
y <- rep(one_ts, 1e6) # instant
```

I'd be happy to contribute a pull request implementing the "merge trick" if that might be the best way to implement a heuristic time saving method in the package.

Hi hadley,

I really appreciate your work for all your packages like ggplot, dplyr, tidyr, lubridate, stringr.

I have a suggestion to add a isoyearweek function in addition to isoweek function:

``` R
isoyearweek <- function (x)
{
  xday <- ISOdate(year(x), month(x), day(x), tz = tz(x))
  dn <- 1 + (wday(x) + 5)%%7
  nth <- xday + ddays(4 - dn)
  jan1 <- ISOdate(year(nth), 1, 1, tz = tz(x))
  weeknum <- 1 + (nth - jan1)%/%ddays(7)

  paste0(isoyear, sprintf("%02d", weeknum))
}
```

Most part is a recopy of your isoweek function, juste add an output to add year info, otherwise a normal `paste0(year(x), isoweek(x))` doesn't work properly.

title: Naming consistency in lubridate
description:
Hi guys,

I have trouble with lubridate naming conventions which I think could be much better.

For example ymd and ymd_hms family of functions return a DateTime object but hms,
hm etc return a period. Besides an obvious user-level inconsistency, Internally
these two famiiles of functions should use completely different parsers.

The singulars date, year etc are accessors/setters for DateTime and Period
objects. Plurals dates, years etc are constructors for Period object. At the
user level this is very confusing as plural/singular convention is pretty
arbitrary. Moreover, there is dyear, dmonth etc which add to the confusion. Why then
not pyear, pmonth for periods?

Here is my proposition. Make the naming consistent and make all of them generic.

Parsers: 

   1) DateTime function tymd, tymdHMS, tHMS etc are parsers and always return
      POSIXct  (HMS, MS, HM fill in the current date).

   2) Period function pS, pM, ph, pHM, pHMS pdHMS etc will parse into
      periods. As compared to thms parser, phms doesn't through an error on
      100:200:1000 type of input.

   3) Duration parsers dS, dM etc 

At the same time all the above functions are generic getters. So that if the input to  `pym` is a POSIXct, or Period, or Duration, then the resulting vector is always a period of years + months. For `tymd` the output is POSIXct whatever the input's class is: POSIX, character, duration etc.

Replacement functions are "ymd", "hms", "H", "M", "S" etc. For example`ym(X) <- object` replaces year and month according to the type of `X`. Class of `X` can be POSIXct, Period, Duration, or even character. It always returns an object of the same class as that of input `X`. That is to say, H, S, M are the replacement on steroids for current hours, minutes, seconds.

I guess it's a significant departure from the current naming conventions, but I wonder what you think.

title: week() function returns a 6 day week at the beginning of a year
description:
There is a bug in the week() function which leads to the first week of the year being only 6 days long. For example, if you type

``` R
x <- seq(from = ymd("2014-01-01"), to = ymd("2014-01-10"), by = "days")
week(x)
```

then you'll get `1 1 1 1 1 1 2 2 2 2`. The code should be changed from it's current state, which is this:

``` R
function(x)
yday(x) %/% 7 + 1
```

to this:

``` R
function(x)
(yday(x) - 1) %/% 7 + 1
```

title: parse_date_time for year and week, no day
description:
Current behavior:

``` r

# [1] "2009-01-12 UTC"
parse_date_time("2009 02", "Y! W")
# [1] "2009-08-21 UTC"
```

So when the day of the week is not given, then you get today's month and day. I am not sure what the result should be, maybe w=1 could be assumed, or an error message, but the current behavior is surely not optimal.

Btw. moment.js parses ISO 8601 weeks without dates, and assumed day = 1:

``` javascript
moment.utc("2009-W02").format()
"2009-01-05T00:00:00+00:00"
```

(But of course it uses ISO weeks, which are different than weeks in lubridate.) So I guess day = 1 would be a reasonable solution.

title: output of as.period in tbl column fails on next filter
description:
The following throws an "Error: column 'period' has unsupported type":

> library(lubridate)
> library(dplyr)
> now0 <- now()
> tmp <- tbl_df(data.frame(period = as.period(now() - now0), test = TRUE))
> filter(tmp, test)

The temporary assignment serves to show that the error really only appears when filter is called.
I'm working around this now by keeping the time interval in the variable and only performing the as.period conversion later in the analysis (in order to be able to do something like: period %/% years(1)), but I suppose it should be possible to do it as above.

title: Wrong timezones for Russia after recent timezone changes
description:
After recent time zone changes in Russia (on the 26th October 2014) the time returned for some Russian cities is incorrect. For example, Moscow is now forever in GMT+3, same as Qatar, however:

``` r
now(tzone = "Europe/Moscow")
```

returns

``` r
"2014-11-05 00:54:03 MSK"
```

while

``` r
now(tzone = "Asia/Qatar")
```

which, as I said, is in the same time zone, returns

``` r
"2014-11-04 23:54:53 AST"
```

The time on the machine is actually 23:54 at the time of code execution. Mac OS X 10.10, time zone set to Moscow Standard Time.

The latest  tz database 2014b seems to reflect these changes:
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones

I suppose they somehow need to be reflected in the lubridate library as well.

Kind regards,
Egor

title: with_tz cacheing results (?) making it incompatible with data.table iteration
description:
I found a weird bug explored more fully in [this gist](https://gist.github.com/Ironholds/c6ddcd7b377844e66803).

TL;DR: when you iterate through a data.table of (timestamp,tz), using unique timezone values as the "by", and apply with_tz, lubridate continues applying the timezone detected in the first subset to all subsequent subsets.

Presumably this is some amount of memoise cacheing; with_tz is not reporting that memoisation is happening, nor responding to forget(), however. Weird! Am I mad or is there a good way of solving this?

title: as.period() Warning becomes Error when stringsAsFactors = FALSE
description:
I've been using this `lubridate`-based function: https://gist.github.com/mmparker/7254445
to calculate ages (in whole years) for several months now, with no problems. But it's started failing recently - ~~possibly because I updated to R 3.1.0, or maybe it's the latest version of lubridate~~ which is somehow related to R 3.1.0.

Basically, when `stringsAsFactors = TRUE`, `as.period()` throws a warning about factors when trying to convert an `Interval`. When `stringsAsFactors = FALSE`, however, it fails completely and throws this mysterious error.

```
Error in FUN(left, right) : non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

Since I'm only passing in Dates, the factors must come into play somewhere within `as.period()` itself.

The code below should help replicate the error. If there's anything else I can do to help, please don't hesitate to let me know. `lubridate` is a great package!

```
library(lubridate)


# Set up some arbitrary birthdates
birthdates <- as.Date(c("1963-01-01", "1983-06-01", "1993-12-31"))


# Calculate intervals to today
age_intervals <- new_interval(birthdates, Sys.Date())


# Convert it to a period and extract the number of years
# First, with stringsAsFactors = TRUE
options(stringsAsFactors = TRUE)

as.period(age_intervals, unit = "year")


# Now try it with stringsAsFactors = FALSE
options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

as.period(age_intervals, unit = "year")
```

title: Behavior of` `ymd_hms()` given conflicting information from `...` and `tz`
description:
Given ISO-8601 formats being supported, it is possible to give conflicting information to `ymd_hms()`.

- "Z" or "-HH:MM" in the string, and
- non-UTC tz

it should return UTC, ignoring tz (currently fails), and issue a warning (currently passes).

Here's some `testthat` verbage:

```
## Inconsistent usage - suppress warning to check return value only
suppressWarnings(
    expect_that(ymd_hms("2012-03-04T05:06:07Z", tz="America/Chicago"), 
                equals(ymd_hms("2012-03-04 05:06:07", tz="UTC")))
)

## Inconsistent usage - check for warning
expect_that(ymd_hms("2012-03-04T05:06:07Z", tz="America/Chicago"), 
            gives_warning("Date in ISO8601 format; timezone ignored"))  
```

title: parse_date_time() returns POSIXlt

The documentation for `parse_date_time()` indicates that it should return "a vector of POSIXct date-time objects" However, this does not seem to be its behavior, instead returning a vector of POSIXlt objects:

```
> dates <- c("2010-1-1", "2012-2-29", "2013-10-21")
> str(parse_date_time(dates, "ymd"))
 POSIXlt[1:3], format: "2010-01-01" "2012-02-29" "2013-10-21"
```

Of course, for this example, using `parse_date_time()` is not necessary, and `ymd()` behaves as expected:

```

 POSIXct[1:3], format: "2010-01-01" "2012-02-29" "2013-10-21"
```

Tested using lubridate 1.3.0 and R 3.0.2

title: Weird behaviour for wday
description:
This is unusual:

```
d_utc <- ymd(20381002, tz='UTC')
d_local <- ymd(20381002, tz='')
wday(d_utc) # 7
wday(d_local) #6
```

I didn't realise the day of the week of a given calendar date depends on the timezone! [/sarcasm]

I believe this odd behaviour is caused by POSIXlt defs in `base`

```
as.POSIXlt(x=d_utc, tz=tz(d_utc))$wday # 6
as.POSIXlt(x=d_local, tz=tz(d_local))$wday # 5
```

Note:
- If I change the calendar date to 5 Oct 2013 I don't see this odd behaviour.
- POSIXlt represents weekdays as numbers from 0 - 6 whereas lubridate's `wday` represents them from 1-7. So POSIXlt wday of 6 is equivalent to lubridate wday of 7.

Does anyone understand POSIXlt is behaving like this? If not I will post bug to [R bug tracking system](http://bugs.r-project.org/) (when it loads - soooo slow!).

title: ymd_hms incorrectly parses "0001-01-01 00:00"
description:
Not sure if this is a bug or feature - but I'll throw it out there 

```
ymd_hms("0001-01-01 00:00")
[1] "2000-01-01 01:00:00 UTC"
```

(I expect `0000-01-01 01:00:00 UTC`); `ymd("0001-01-01")` also works, but it would be nice if `ymd("01-01-01")` also did, although I realize that this is a unique case.

But it does matter because the ncep climate reanalysis data has a time dimension defined as "hours since 01-01-01" (example file can be [downloaded here](http://file-server.igb.illinois.edu/~dlebauer/1948.nc)). 

Interestingly the metadata (from [NOAA](http://www.esrl.noaa.gov/psd/data/gridded/data.ncep.reanalysis.html)) say that 1948-01-01 is 117067072 hours since 0001-01-01. By contrast, `ymd("0001-01-01") + hours(17067072)` returns "1948-01-03 UTC".

title: Remove as.POSIXct from tests
description:
The behavior of as.POSIXct changes in R devel. Previously

```
as.POSIXct("2010-11-07 01:59:59", tz = "America/New_York")
[1] "2010-11-07 01:59:59 EST"
```

Hereforth

```
as.POSIXct("2010-11-07 01:59:59", tz = "America/New_York")
[1] "2010-11-07 01:59:59 EDT"
```

In otherwords, when a clock time occurs during the fall DST overlap, as.POSIXct will start assigning it to the earlier of the two matching times instead of the latter. At the moment, tests that use as.POSIXct will not simultaneously pass CRAN checks against 3.0.0 and R devel.

A more robust way to create POSIXct objects for testing is with `structure`

title: Proposal: support for ISO-8601
description:
```
library("lubridate")

#' @source \url{http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601}
#' @source \url{http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601_usage}
```
### Rationale

ISO 8601 covers the exchange of date and time related data. For me, personally, it is a format that I am seeing more-and-more, such that it may be useful to offer an extension to lubridate. For me, I receive date/times as ISO-8601 strings and also have to send back date-times as ISO-8601 strings.

ISO-8601 is used to describe instants, durations, and time-spans, although it does not  seem to make the distinction between periods and durations in the way that lubridate does. Of course, I may not know enough about ISO-8601 to comment credibly.
### Current state

It is entirely possible that a great majority of the use of ISO-8601 is to describe instants. The ymd_hms function works for the first case, but fails the second case:

```
# creating an instant    
my_dtm <- ymd_hms("2012-11-19T17:00:00Z") # succeeds
my_dtm2 <- ymd_hms("2012-11-19T17:00:00+01:00") # fails
```

To format a date-time in an ISO-8601 format seems straightforward using the "Z" convention for UTC, but it is unclear to me how express this using the offset of the timezone (or even if it is important to do so).

```
# formatting an instant
format(with_tz(my_dtm, tzone="UTC"), "%y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ") # specifying UTC
```
### Possible future state

If we know that we are working with an ISO-8601 string, it seems possible (if not efficient) to assume that a computer could parse the string without hints as to its contents. It may make sense to start with instant and then extend to duration/period and interval.

There are doubtless better names for methods than the ones I outline here. I use these only because you have to start somewhere.

```
#' from_iso_8601
#' 
#' @param  str_iso_8601   string describing instant, duration, or interval
#' 
#' @return                lubridate instant, duration, interval   

#' from_iso_8601.instant
#' 
#' @param  str_iso_8601   string describing instant
#' 
#' @return                lubridate instant
```

When we go to ISO-8601 from an instant/duration/interval, it would seem necessary to specify a format. 

```
#' to_iso_8601
#' 
#' @param  dtm            lubridate instant, duration, interval           
#' @param  format         string describing format       
#' 
#' @return                string describing lubridate instant, duration, interval   

#' to_iso_8601.instant
#' 
#' @param  dtm            lubridate instant         
#' @param  format         string describing format: "Z" (UTC) or "offset" (using tz of dtm)       
#' 
#' @return                string describing lubridate instant  
```
### Next steps?

I am happy to take a stab at coding up a few things, and then let the community do it properly. I suspect that instant would cover a lot of the need, but my perspective is limited.

title: Hour etc should work with periods
Behavior of period through daylight-saving interface
description:
### Edit: This is not an error - this is the user not understanding properly

In the US, daylight-saving time for 2013 begins on the morning of March 10.

If I step through the first hours of that day using durations to represent hours, I get the right answers; if I use periods to represent hours, I get wrong answers.

``` r
> dtm_start <- ymd("2013-03-10", tz="America/Chicago")
> dtm_start + seq(1,3)*dhours(1) # duration
[1] "2013-03-10 01:00:00 CST" "2013-03-10 03:00:00 CDT" "2013-03-10 04:00:00 CDT"
> dtm_start + seq(1,3)*hours(1) # period
[1] "2013-03-10 01:00:00 CST" NA                        "2013-03-10 03:00:00 CDT" 
```

For sake of completeness, there also appears a problem using period when daylight-saving time ends (Nov. 3):

``` r
> dtm_start <- ymd("2013-11-03", tz="America/Chicago")
> dtm_start + seq(1,3)*dhours(1) # duration
[1] "2013-11-03 01:00:00 CDT" "2013-11-03 01:00:00 CST" "2013-11-03 02:00:00 CST"
> dtm_start + seq(1,3)*hours(1) # period
[1] "2013-11-03 01:00:00 CDT" "2013-11-03 02:00:00 CST" "2013-11-03 03:00:00 CST"
```

Happy to poke around, but I wanted first to raise the issue. It is entirely possible, even likely, that this is the intended behavior and I am abusing periods. If so, apologies.

title: Proposal: Support for different Calendar Systems

So because 1371/2/31 is considered the 31 of February, it is changed to NA.

I think this might be a big concern for all people using non-Gregorian calendars. 

(See this http://www.fourmilab.ch/documents/calendar/ )

I propose that working with several different calendar systems be implemented in lubridate. They can be saved internally as Gregorian dates.

I have a little experience in R, i can read and understand various C/C++, JavaScript, ... codes out there which can be used to do the conversions.  and I have experience creating an R package, but I know nothing about git/GitHub and how to use it. I will try to help if needed.

title: Optimization for interval()
description:
Inside the `interval()` constructor function, there's a call to `with_tz()` to ensure the timezone is set correctly.  This can be a very expensive call, because it converts the object by `POSIXct -> POSIXlt -> POSIXct`, or by `POSIXlt -> POSIXct -> POSIXlt`.

The simplest fix would be to protect that `with_tz` call with an `if (tzone != tz(starts))` check, so it's only invoked when a change is actually necessary.

Additionally, `with_tz()` could be optimized when given a `POSIXct` object to not create an intermediate `POSIXlt` object, for further benefits.

title: Getting the number of days in the month
description:
Occasionally it is useful to know how many days there are in each month.  For example, if you have monthly readings of something (sales totals or electricity consumption or whatever), you might expect there to be less in February since the month is shorter.  In this case it can be useful to normalise the monthly readings by dividing by the number of days in that month.

Here's a suggested implementation

```
#' Get the number of days in the month of a date-time.
#' 
#' Date-time must be a POSIXct, POSIXlt, Date, chron, yearmon, yearqtr, 
#' zoo, zooreg, timeDate, xts, its, ti, jul, timeSeries, and fts objects.
#'
#' @param x a date-time object
#' @return An integer of the number of days in the month component of the date-time object.
days_in_month <- function(x)
{
  month_x <- month(x, label = TRUE)
  N_DAYS <- c(
    Jan = 31L, Feb = 28L, Mar = 31L, 
    Apr = 30L, May = 31L, Jun = 30L, 
    Jul = 31L, Aug = 31L, Sep = 30L, 
    Oct = 31L, Nov = 30L, Dec = 31L
  )
  n_days <- N_DAYS[month_x]
  n_days[month_x == "Feb" & leap_year(x)] <- 29L
  n_days
}
```

And some `testthat`-style tests.

```
context("test days_in_month")

test_that(
  "days in month works for non leap years",
  {
    x <- seq(ymd("2011-01-01"), ymd("2011-12-01"), "1 month")
    expected <- c(
      Jan = 31L, Feb = 28L, Mar = 31L, 
      Apr = 30L, May = 31L, Jun = 30L, 
      Jul = 31L, Aug = 31L, Sep = 30L, 
      Oct = 31L, Nov = 30L, Dec = 31L
    )
    expect_that(days_in_month(x), equals(expected))
  }
)

test_that(
  "days in month works for leap years",
  {
    x <- seq(ymd("2012-01-01"), ymd("2012-12-01"), "1 month")
    expected <- c(
      Jan = 31L, Feb = 29L, Mar = 31L, 
      Apr = 30L, May = 31L, Jun = 30L, 
      Jul = 31L, Aug = 31L, Sep = 30L, 
      Oct = 31L, Nov = 30L, Dec = 31L
    )
    expect_that(days_in_month(x), equals(expected))
  }
)
```

So, my thought was that using this option, mdy would return the same values regardless whether quiet is T or F. The only difference is whether you get diagnostic notes printed to the terminal. That does not seem to be the case, however.

> library(lubridate)
> mdy("09-06-12")
> Multiple format matches with 1 successes: %m-%d-%y, %m-%d-%Y.
> [1] "2012-09-06 UTC"
> mdy("09-06-12", quiet = TRUE)
> [1] "2012-09-06 UTC" "0012-09-06 UTC"

Particularly problematic for me is that I called mdy on a vector of dates with quiet = TRUE and it just replaced values so I did not actually get an error! I just was confused on why I was getting weird results. 

Anyway, for now I am just going to return mdy("09-06-12", quiet = FALSE). But like I said, I can't decide if this is a bug, feature, or poor documentation. On the one hand, I could see the quiet option not having any impact on what is returned, so in that case it is a bug. The feature is that if you don't tell the person what you are doing you want to return all options, so in that case it is a feature. While the documentation is correct in that it does not display, it is misleading because this option changes the return values, so in that case it is poor documentation. 

At the very least, I think the documentation should be changed to be more clear that the return value is different.

title: Adding `months` periods to end of month instant badness
description:
Loving `lubridate`. However, there are a few bugs I've noticed. One of which is the following.

Suppose we have the end of a month instant:
`date3 <- ymd("2012-07-31")`

Now suppose that wewould like to find the instant one (period) month from `date3`:
`date3 + months(1)   # "2012-08-31 UTC"`

_This looks right_.

Now suppose that we would like to find the instant two (period) months from `date3`:
`date3 + months(2)   # "2012-10-01 UTC"`

_This looks wrong_. 

The common behaviour for this sort of operation should be to return the last day of the month when the original date is the 31st of a month. Otherwise it should return the same `mday` for month `N` (period) months from the original date. I've coded the behaviour I would expect here:

```
shiftDateByNMonths <- function (date1, N) {

  N <- as.integer(N)

  if (is.na(N)) {

    stop ("Your N is bigger in modulus than the largest integer. Try again.")

  }

  year  <- year(date1)
  month <- month(date1)
  day   <- mday(date1)

  iYear  <- year
  iMonth <- month + N
  iDay   <- day

  while ((iMonth > 12) | (iMonth <= 0)){
    iMonth <- iMonth - sign(N) * 12
    iYear  <- iYear + sign(N) * 1 
  }

  lastDay <- getDaysInMonth(ymd(paste(iYear, iMonth, 1, sep="-")))

  if (iDay > lastDay) {
    iDay <- lastDay
  } 

  shiftedDate <- ymd(paste(iYear, iMonth, iDay, sep="-"))

  return (shiftedDate)

}
```

This function's test cases (and results) are:

```
date3 <- ymd("2011-02-28")
shiftDateByNMonths(date3, 1) # "2011-03-28 UTC"
date3 <- ymd("2012-02-29")
shiftDateByNMonths(date3, 1) # "2012-03-29 UTC"
date3 <- ymd("2012-04-30")
shiftDateByNMonths(date3, 1) # "2012-05-30 UTC"
date3 <- ymd("2012-03-31")
shiftDateByNMonths(date3, 1) # "2012-04-30 UTC"
```

Hope that clarifies what I would expect. Love to hear feedback. Perhaps I misunderstood the definition of a `period` (as per "Dates and Times Made Easy with lubridate", Apr 2011)

title: reclass_date() issue
description:
Using our new accessor settor scheme, we turn a date-time object to a POSIX object, manipulate it and then use reclass_date() to send it back to its original class. This has the unintentional side effect of erasing any manipulations not supported by that class. For example,

today() + minutes(10) + seconds(10)

will return the same thing as 

today()

because today() is a Date class object, which does not support time units less than a day. 

Do either of the options below appeal to you?
1. keep it like this. Require users to change a date-time object to a class that supports their goals before they start manipulating it, or
2. remove the reclass_date() step. Manipulating dates would automatically convert them to a POSIXt object, which is very versatile. Users would have to manually convert it back to their class if they wish to do so.

Our previous method automatically converted Date objects to POSIXct objects when hours, minutes, or seconds were added, but ignored the issue for other classes.

Unfortunately it's not possible to just implement a `length.period` method, because then all kinds of mayhem happens when various other `period` methods (and probably various other R functions outside lubridate) use the `length()` method and expect it to return the number of columns (even though they should probably use `ncol` instead).

I'm wondering what could be done about this - the obvious thing would be to rotate the internal data frame 90 degrees, but since the `seconds` component can be non-integer, that means _all_ components would potentially turn into floats.

Any other thoughts?  It ends up impeding the person who wants to use periods in various ways - for example it can't usefully be an argument to `lapply` and friends.

Nanu Frechen

title: Detecting overlapping intervals
description:
It seems to be a moderately common problem to want to know whether two time intervals overlap.  There currently isn't (AFAIK) a function in lubridate to do this.  I suggest the following implementation, based on the algorithm [here](stackoverflow.com/questions/325933/determine-whether-two-date-ranges-overlap).

```
int_overlaps <- function(int1, int2)
{
  (int_start(int1) <= int_end(int2)) & 
  (int_start(int2) <= int_end(int1))
}

int1 <- new_interval(ymd("2012-01-01"), ymd("2012-01-10"))
int2 <- new_interval(ymd("2012-01-06"), ymd("2012-01-15"))
int3 <- new_interval(ymd("2012-01-11"), ymd("2012-01-20"))
int_overlaps(c(int1, int1, int2), c(int2, int3, int3))
```

title: add_period_to_interval gives unintuitive result
description:
Currently adding a period to an interval extends the length of the interval, whereas it seems more intuitive to shift the whole interval.

For example, 

```
new_interval(ymd("2012-01-02"), ymd("2012-01-06")) + weeks(1:4)
```

currently returns

```
[1] 2012-01-02 -- 2012-01-13  2012-01-02 -- 2012-01-20 
[3] 2012-01-02 -- 2012-01-27  2012-01-02 -- 2012-02-03
```

and not the weekdays in January this year as expected.

Suggested new implementation.

```
add_period_to_interval <- function (per, int) 
{
  start <- int_start(int)
  end <- int_end(int)
  new_interval(end + per, start + per)
}
```

title: how to work with date ranges greater than 16 years?
description:
lubridate calculates the difference between dates in seconds
a <- now() # "2009-07-27 11:01:12 CDT"

> z <- now() #"2009-07-27 11:01:19 CDT"
> z - a = 6.10436415672302 seconds

This difference is automatically stored as a duration. Since durations cannot handle intervals greater than 5e+08 seconds, we cannot subtract dates more than ~16 years apart.

a <- a + 250000001   # "2017-06-28 23:27:53 CDT"
z <- z - 250000011 # "2001-08-24 22:34:28 CDT"

z - a = Error in new_duration(second = as.numeric(x, units = "secs")) : seconds overflow: see 'duration' documentation

This limits the date combinations that we can subtract, but also hampers pretty.date() for date ranges greater than 16 years.

title: how to handle data.frames of duration objects?
description:
Since a duration is also a data.frame, putting it into data structures that do not retain its class attributes converts it back into a data frame without warning.
1. putting durations into a vector with c() creates a list where each element is alternatively a $months or $seconds value

we can prevent this or insert  warning by writing a c.duration() but this will not be called if the first element in the vector is not a duration.
1. putting durations into a list with list() creates a list where each element is a duration
2. putting durations into a data.frame with data.frame() drops the duration class and cbinds the remaining 1 x 2 dataframes

Which of these would we like to users to use with durations, and what do we want the output ot look like?

title: Create new duration format
description:
Instead of storing durations as data.frames, store them as atomic numbers where the 9 rightmost digits are seconds and the remainder are months.

Blocks of 126239400 seconds can be converted to four years, since this is the number of seconds in three years and a leap year.  This will prevent the number of seconds from spilling into the months columns. (An exception will have to be made for years like 2000 which should be leap years but are not.  I'm still thinking about this.)

This change will require:
- a new print_duration function
- new as.duration(), is.duration(), new_duration() and related functions
- new Ops functions (+, -, /, *)
- the new ops functions seem to require new accessor functions for the durations (for example, second(duration))

title: identify and handle four year periods with no leap years

the durations format automatically prevents seconds data from spilling into months data by moving four year blocks of seconds to the months side.  This works because 3 years + 1 leap year is (normally) a fixed number of seconds.

Sometimes, however, a four year block does not have a leap year (for example 2000).  I nthis case the duration will be 1 day too long.  

I need to create a way to test for this and fix it.
